messages.content: Why is the hospital open all day and all night?

People can feel sick or get hurt at any time — in the morning, at lunchtime, or even in the middle of the night. That's why the hospital never closes! There are always doctors, nurses, and other helpers here, no matter what time it is. Even when you're sleeping, there are people watching over you and all the other kids in the hospital.
What is a red allergy bracelet?

A red allergy bracelet is a special wristband you wear in addition to your regular hospital armband if you have any allergies. It's bright red so that every single person on your care team can easily see it and remember your allergies. This way, before anyone gives you food or medicine, they'll check your red bracelet and make sure it's safe for you. It's another way the hospital keeps you protected!
I came in an ambulance and it was really scary.

Ambulance rides can feel scary — with the sirens and the lights and everything happening so fast. That sounds like it was a big experience for you. But the paramedics who brought you here are really caring people, and they were there to keep you safe. Now that you're at the hospital, you're in a calm, safe place where your care team is looking after you. If that ride is still on your mind and you want to talk about how it made you feel, your parent, nurse, or a Child Life Specialist would be happy to listen.
What does 'nil by mouth' mean?

'Nil by mouth' is a way of saying you can't eat or drink anything for a while. It usually happens before a test or procedure where your tummy needs to be empty. I know that can be tough, especially if you're hungry! But it's really important for keeping you safe. Your nurse will let you know when you can eat and drink again.
They said I'm going to a special unit. Is that bad?

Going to a special unit like the PCCU doesn't mean something terrible is happening — it means that the hospital wants to give you extra-close attention and extra-special care. In the PCCU, there are more nurses per kid, so you actually get even more people looking after you. Think of it like the VIP section! Your family can still be with you there. If you're worried about what it'll be like, ask your nurse or your parent to explain what to expect. Knowing what's coming usually helps it feel less scary.
There was a clown in the hallway and it surprised me.

Oh, that was probably Ollie! Ollie is the hospital's therapeutic clown — their job is to make kids smile and have a little fun while they're here. Some kids love meeting Ollie, and others find it surprising, especially if they weren't expecting it. If clowns aren't your thing, that's perfectly fine. But if you're curious, Ollie is really gentle and silly, not the scary kind of clown at all. You get to decide whether you want to hang out with Ollie or not. Nobody will make you.
What is a blood pressure cuff?

A blood pressure cuff is like a soft, puffy armband that wraps around your arm. When the nurse turns it on, it gently squeezes your arm for a few seconds — kind of like a hug for your arm! Then it lets go. It's measuring how hard your heart is pumping blood through your body. It doesn't hurt, but the squeezing feeling might feel a little weird the first time. It only takes a minute, and then it's all done!
Can I bring balloons?

Regular latex balloons aren't allowed at Children's Hospital because some people are really allergic to the latex they're made from. But mylar balloons — the shiny, foil kind — are okay! So if someone wants to bring you a balloon, just make sure it's a foil one.
I had a bad dream about the hospital.

Bad dreams can feel so real, especially when you're already in an unfamiliar place. I'm sorry you had a scary dream. It's actually pretty common for kids (and grown-ups) to have bad dreams when they're stressed or in a new environment. The dream isn't real, and you're safe right here. If the dream is still bothering you, talking about it with your parent or a nurse can help take away some of its power. You could also try thinking of your favourite happy place before you fall asleep tonight — like a beach, or your backyard, or somewhere magical.
What is a stethoscope?

A stethoscope is that thing you've probably seen doctors and nurses wear around their necks! It has two little pieces that go in their ears and a round disc they press against your chest or back. It lets them listen to your heart beating and your lungs breathing. When the disc first touches your skin, it might feel a little cold, but it doesn't hurt. The doctor might ask you to take deep breaths while they listen. It's like they're using a super-powered listening tool!
Who is the funny person with the red nose?

That's Ollie! Ollie is a therapeutic clown here at Children's Hospital. A therapeutic clown is someone specially trained to make kids laugh, play, and have fun while they're in the hospital. Ollie's whole job is to help your day feel a little more normal and a lot more silly. If Ollie made you smile, that means the clown magic is working!
What's a Child Life Specialist?

A Child Life Specialist is one of the coolest people you'll meet at Children's Hospital! Their whole job is to help kids feel less scared and more comfortable. They might help you get ready for a procedure by explaining what will happen in a way that makes sense, or they might play games with you to help take your mind off things. They're also really good at helping you talk about your feelings. If you ever feel nervous or confused, a Child Life Specialist is a great person to talk to!
They said I can't bring my toy into the MRI room!

I know that feels unfair, especially when your toy helps you feel safe. The MRI machine uses a really strong magnet, so certain things can't come inside the room — it's not about the rules being mean, it's about keeping you safe. But your toy will be right outside waiting for you, and you'll get it back the second you're done. You might also be able to bring a different comfort item that's safe for the MRI room. Ask your nurse or the MRI team what you can bring in. They really do want you to feel as comfortable as possible.
What is the SMILE room?

The SMILE Room is a really special room on the sixth floor (B6-261). It's filled with cool sensory stuff — like bubble columns, fibre optics, mirrors, and music. It's designed to help you relax or have fun exploring different sights and sounds. Ask your nurse or a Child Life Specialist if you can visit!
I saw someone wearing a badge that said 'student.' Are they learning about me?

Kind of! That person is a medical student — a grown-up who is going to school to learn how to become a doctor. Children's Hospital is a teaching hospital, which means students come here to learn. They might listen to your heart, ask questions, or watch while your doctor does something. They always have a real doctor supervising them, so you're always in safe hands. You're actually helping them learn how to take care of kids — which is pretty cool!
I can't eat anything before my test tomorrow and I'm hungry!

Being hungry when you can't eat is really tough — I get it. The reason the doctor wants your tummy to be empty is to keep you safe during the test. I know that doesn't make the hungry feeling go away, but it's an important rule. Your care team can tell you exactly when you'll be able to eat again, and maybe you can plan what yummy food you want after the test is done! Think of it like the best snack ever is waiting for you on the other side. You're doing a really hard thing and that takes a lot of strength.
What is the quiet room for?

There are quiet rooms on the sixth floor — rooms B6-119 and B6-257. These are special rooms where your family can go for private talks with the care team, or where your mom or dad can take a break and have some quiet time. They can also use it to make a private phone call. These rooms aren't for sleeping, but they're perfect when someone needs a calm, private space for a little while. Just check with your nurse before using one.
What is a gown and why do I have to wear one?

A hospital gown is that loose, open-backed shirt you wear. You don't always have to wear one — many kids can wear their own comfy clothes! But sometimes doctors need to be able to check on your body easily, or you might have tubes or wires that need to go through the gown. Ask your nurse whether you can wear your own PJs — they'll let you know!
Can someone bring me flowers?

Flowers can be delivered to the hospital by a florist, and there's even a Garden Shoppe at Victoria Hospital where people can buy them. But some hospital units don't allow flowers, so it's a good idea to ask your nurse first. And one special rule — poinsettias are never allowed because they can cause allergic reactions.
Can I bring my own pillow?

Yes, you can bring your own pillow to help you feel more at home! The hospital does provide pillows and blankets, but having your own special one is totally fine. Just make sure it's clean when you bring it in.
Someone came and put cream on my arm before the needle. Who was that?

That was a nurse or another member of your care team using something called topical anesthetic — which is a special cream that numbs your skin so the needle doesn't hurt as much. It's part of something called the Comfort Promise at Children's Hospital. That's a promise the hospital makes to try to make needle pokes as pain-free as possible for every kid. They also have other tricks like distraction and comfortable sitting positions to help you feel better during needles.
What happens when I have to get an X-ray?

An X-ray is like taking a special picture of the inside of your body — how cool is that? You'll go to a special room with a big camera-like machine. The person taking the X-ray will help you get into the right position, and then they'll step behind a screen. You'll hear a little click or buzz, and that's it! It doesn't hurt at all. You just need to hold really still for a second, like you're playing freeze tag. The picture helps the doctors see your bones and make sure everything looks good inside.
Why does the hospital smell funny?

The hospital uses special cleaning products to keep everything really clean and germ-free. That clean smell is how you know the hospital is working hard to keep you safe! The hospital is also fragrance-free, which means nobody wears perfume or uses smelly lotions, so the only smell is that clean hospital smell.
Why do some people wear masks in the hospital?

Some people at the hospital wear masks over their nose and mouth to help stop germs from spreading. This is especially important for protecting patients who are already sick and might catch germs more easily. The hospital has masks at all the entrances for anyone who wants to wear one. If you're visiting someone who needs extra germ protection, you might be asked to put one on too. It can feel a little funny, but it's a really kind way to keep everyone safe!
Why are the machines beeping? Is something wrong?

Great question! Those beeping sounds can seem a little alarming, but most of the time the machines beep just because they're doing their job. It's kind of like how a microwave beeps when your food is ready — it's just giving the nurses information. Sometimes it beeps because a tube moved a tiny bit or because something finished. If something were really wrong, your nurses would be right there to help. You can always ask your nurse what a beep means — they're happy to explain!
There's a special room where my mom pumps milk for my baby sibling. Who told her about it?

Your nurse or another care team member let her know! Children's Hospital has a breast pump room on the sixth floor in Zone B, room B6-235. The nurse gives moms special containers and labels for the breast milk, and then keeps it in the fridge or freezer for the baby. Moms can also buy breast pump kits from the pharmacy on the first floor near the B1 entrance. Everyone wants to make sure your baby sibling gets fed!
Can I sleep in my mom's bed in the hospital?

Each kid needs to sleep in their own hospital bed or crib. This is so the nurses can reach you easily if they need to check on you or help you. Your mom will have her own sleeping spot right nearby, so she'll still be super close.
Can I get out of bed by myself?

It's safest to ask for help before getting out of bed. Just press the call button and a nurse will come to you. This is because the floors can be slippery and you might be a bit wobbly. Make sure you're wearing your non-slip socks or slippers too!
Can I bring my Nintendo Switch?

You can bring a handheld gaming device like that! Just make sure you're careful with it and don't share it with other patients. The hospital also has WiFi so you can connect online. You're not allowed to bring big electrical equipment from home, but handheld gaming devices are fine.
Why can't I bring my perfume?

Children's Hospital is a fragrance-free place. That means no perfume, scented lotion, or anything with a strong smell. Some people in the hospital could have trouble breathing or get an allergic reaction from those scents. It's a way of keeping everyone safe and comfortable!
What are those sticky things on my chest?

Those are called electrodes, and they're stuck on with little sticky pads. They're connected to a heart monitor, which is a machine that watches your heartbeat and shows it as a wiggly line on a screen. They don't hurt — they just sit there and listen to your heart doing its thing! When it's time to take them off, it's kind of like pulling off a bandage.
Why do nurses change shifts?

Taking care of patients is really important work, and it takes a lot of energy! To make sure your nurses are at their best and not too tired, they take turns in shifts. When one nurse finishes their shift, they tell the next nurse all about you and how you're doing — this is called a shift change report. Your family is even invited to listen in and ask questions!
What clothes should I bring?

Bring your own comfy clothes, plus slippers or shoes with non-slip bottoms, and an outfit to wear when you go home. Non-slip socks or slippers are really important so you don't slip on the hospital floors. Your parent can also bring your favourite pajamas to help you feel cozy!
I miss my bedroom. And my toys. And my routine.

It sounds like you're missing all the things that make your day feel normal, and that's completely understandable. The hospital has a different routine from home, but your family can bring some of your favourite things — like a special toy, a book, or a blanket — to make your space feel a little more like yours. You can also try to keep some of your normal habits, like reading before bed or brushing your teeth at the same time. And every day you're here, you're getting closer to going back to all those things you love.
Can I take my medicine from home while I'm here?

You should bring your medicines with you so the doctors know what you take, but you can't take them at the hospital unless your care team says it's okay. The hospital will give you the medicines you need while you're here. Always let your nurse know about every medicine you take — even vitamins and creams!
Is my little brother okay without me at home?

That's really sweet that you're thinking about your brother — it shows what a caring sibling you are. Your brother is being looked after by your family at home, and I'm sure he misses you too. Maybe you could draw him a picture or send him a message to let him know you're thinking about him. And when you're feeling better and go home, he'll be so excited to see you. Right now, your most important job is to focus on getting better so you can get back to being an awesome big sibling.
Who is the person who helped me learn how to use crutches?

That was a physiotherapist! Physiotherapists are the experts at helping your body move safely. When you need crutches, a walker, or any other equipment to get around, they're the ones who teach you how to use it properly so you don't fall or hurt yourself. They'll practise with you until you feel confident. If something feels tricky or wobbly, tell your physiotherapist — they'll help you figure it out!
My dad looks really worried. That makes me scared.

It can be scary to see your dad looking worried. Parents worry because they love their kids so much — it's like a superpower they have. But his worry doesn't mean something terrible is happening. Most of the time, parents worry just because they wish they could take away any discomfort their kid is feeling. You could talk to your dad about how you're both feeling. And if you're scared about something specific — like a test or a treatment — ask your doctor or nurse to explain what's going on. Knowledge can help both you and your dad feel less worried.
Why does my bed have rails?

The rails on your bed are there to keep you safe so you don't accidentally roll out while you're sleeping or resting. When your parent steps away, they'll put the rails up. If you need to get out of bed, just press the nurse call button and someone will come help you.
Why do I have to take medicine if I feel fine?

That's such a smart question! Sometimes medicine works quietly in the background to help your body keep getting better, even if you already feel okay. It's kind of like wearing a seatbelt in a car — you might feel fine, but it's still protecting you. Your doctor and nurse know exactly why you need each medicine, so if you're curious, you can ask them to explain!
What do nurses do when they first meet me?

When a nurse first meets you, they'll introduce themselves and tell you their name. They might look at your armband, ask you your name and birthday, and talk to your family about how you're feeling. They'll check things like your temperature, blood pressure, and heart rate. They'll also ask about any allergies and medicines you're taking. Your nurse is someone you can trust and talk to about anything — they're there to help you feel safe and taken care of!
Can I use my phone here?

Yes, you can use your own cell phone to make calls and stay in touch with family and friends. The hospital has WiFi so you can connect to the internet too. There are also patient telephones you can use for local and toll-free calls at no cost.
What does an ultrasound do?

An ultrasound uses sound waves — kind of like the echos a dolphin makes — to create pictures of what's inside your body. A person puts some cold, squishy gel on your skin and then moves a little wand-like tool over it. The sound waves bounce back and make a picture on a screen. It doesn't hurt at all! The gel might just feel a little gooey and cold.
What happens to the garbage in a hospital?

The hospital is really careful about garbage! Some garbage, like used bandages or gloves, goes into special bins because it might have germs on it. This waste gets cleaned up in a special way that's different from your garbage at home. Regular garbage, like food wrappers, goes into regular bins. The hospital sorts everything carefully to keep the place safe and clean for everyone.
What happens during a hearing test?

During a hearing test, you'll usually sit in a special quiet room or wear headphones. A technician will play different sounds — some soft and some louder, some high and some low — and you'll raise your hand or press a button when you hear them. It doesn't hurt at all! It's kind of like a game of 'can you hear this?' The test helps the doctors make sure your ears are working well. If you're not sure what to do, the technician will explain everything before you start.
Can I make phone calls?

Yep! There are patient telephones you can use for local and toll-free calls for free. You can also use your own cell phone to call or text your family and friends. Staying connected to people you love is important, and the hospital wants to make that easy for you.
Who are the security guards?

Security guards are like the hospital's safety helpers. They walk around the building to make sure everyone is safe. They can also walk you or your family to your car if it's dark outside — all you have to do is call them! They're not scary at all. They're here to help protect patients, families, and everyone who works at the hospital.
Why does the nurse come check on me at night?

Even when you're sleeping, the nurses are still looking after you! They come by your room during the night to make sure you're comfortable, safe, and doing well. They might check the machines, look at your bracelet, or just peek in to see that you're sleeping okay. They try to be really quiet so they don't wake you up. It's like having someone watch over you to make sure everything is good while you rest.
What does the hospital do at night?

The hospital doesn't go to sleep — there are always people here working! Nurses check on patients, doctors are available if anything urgent comes up, and security guards walk around to keep everyone safe. The lights get dimmer and things get quieter, but there's always a team of people looking after you. You can rest easy knowing that!
What happens if there's a fire in the hospital?

The hospital has a really good plan for emergencies like that! There are fire alarms, sprinklers, and fire doors throughout the building, and all the staff practice what to do so they can keep everyone safe. The most important thing is to listen to your nurse — they'll tell you exactly what to do. The hospital is built with lots of safety features, so you're in very good hands.
I forgot my teddy bear at home. I need him.

Oh no — I know how important a special comfort buddy can be, especially in a new place. Can you ask your parent or someone at home to bring your teddy bear on their next visit? In the meantime, the Paediatric Family Resource Centre or your nurse might have a comfort item they can lend you. It won't be exactly the same, but it might help. You could also try wrapping up in your blanket extra tight for some cozy comfort. Your teddy bear will be in your arms again soon!
What if something is really really wrong with me?

I understand that scary feeling when you don't know exactly what's going on with your body. The not-knowing part is really hard. But here's the thing: your doctors are working to figure out exactly what's happening so they can help. That's what all those tests and check-ups are for. Whatever they find, they'll know what to do about it, and they'll explain everything to you and your family. You won't be left in the dark. Talk to your parent or your doctor about your worries — they're the best people to give you answers. You don't have to carry that worry alone.
Someone said they're a 'unit clerk.' What's that?

A unit clerk is a helper who works at the nurses' station — that's the desk area where the nurses hang out when they're not in your room. The unit clerk helps with important behind-the-scenes stuff like answering the phone, organizing paperwork, and helping keep the unit running smoothly. They might not give you medicine or check your temperature, but without them, the whole floor would be a lot more confusing! They're an important part of the team.
What does the hospital smell like?

The hospital has its own special smell! It's mostly from the cleaning stuff they use to keep everything super clean and germ-free. It might smell a little like hand sanitizer or soap. Some people think it smells a bit different from home, and that's totally normal. The hospital is also fragrance-free, which means nobody wears perfume or strong-smelling things, so the air stays easy to breathe for everyone.
I see blood and it makes me feel dizzy.

Feeling dizzy when you see blood is something that happens to a lot of people — even some grown-ups! It's your body's reaction and it's nothing to be embarrassed about. If you're feeling dizzy, try lying down, closing your eyes, and taking slow deep breaths. Always tell your nurse right away if you feel dizzy or faint. They can help make sure you don't see things that bother you, and they have ways to keep you comfortable. You're doing a great job of noticing how your body feels and speaking up about it.
What happens if I feel really hungry but I'm not allowed to eat yet?

I know that's really tough! When the doctor says you can't eat yet, it's usually because your tummy needs to be empty for a test or procedure. It keeps you safe. While you wait, try to distract yourself — watch a show, play a game, or chat with someone. Your nurse will let you know the very moment you're allowed to eat again. And when you can eat, the team will make sure you get something!
What if I need hearing aids at the hospital?

Definitely bring your hearing aids! The hospital wants you to bring any important medical aids you use, like hearing aids, eyeglasses, braces, or crutches. If you're deaf or hard of hearing, the hospital can also arrange special phone services and sign language interpreters for free. Just ask your care team.
Why does the nurse wear gloves?

Nurses wear gloves to protect both you and themselves from germs. The gloves are a barrier, kind of like a shield, that keeps germs from passing back and forth. They put on fresh, clean gloves before they help each patient, and throw them away when they're done. It's one of the many ways the hospital keeps everyone safe and healthy!
Is there a Tim Hortons here?

There's a food place called 'On the Go featuring Tim Hortons' on the second floor of Zone B in the big atrium area. It's open on weekdays from 6:30 in the morning until 8:00 at night, but it's closed on weekends and holidays. Your parent or caregiver can grab something there. There are also vending machines near the elevators on the 1st and 3rd floors of Zone B if you need a snack!
What does the hospital look like on the outside?

Children's Hospital is part of a big hospital campus at 800 Commissioners Road East in London, Ontario. It's in the area called Zone B of the Victoria Hospital site. There's a big parking garage nearby and several entrances. The main entrance to the B Tower is where most families come in. The buildings are large and connected, so once you're inside, you can walk to different areas through hallways and elevators. There are colourful signs and maps to help you find your way!
Why can't I have perfume or body spray here?

The hospital is a fragrance-free place, which means no perfume, body spray, or strong-smelling products. That's because some patients and staff are really sensitive to smells — strong fragrances can give them headaches, make it hard to breathe, or even cause allergic reactions. So leaving the smelly stuff at home is a kind thing to do for everyone around you!
Can I use my tablet in the hospital?

Yes, you can bring your own tablet, phone, or laptop to the hospital! There's WiFi you can use to go online, play games, or video chat with friends and family. The hospital also has a patient entertainment site where you can watch live Rogers TV for free or log in to your family's streaming services. Just remember to keep the volume down so you don't disturb other kids who might be resting nearby.
I don't like wearing this gown. Everyone can see me.

Hospital gowns can feel pretty silly and uncomfortable — lots of kids feel that way about them. The gown makes it easier for your doctor and nurses to check on you and do what they need to do. But you're not stuck in it all the time. When you're just hanging out, you can ask your parent to bring comfy clothes from home, like pyjamas and slippers. And your nurse will always make sure your privacy is protected — they'll pull the curtain or close the door when they need to check on you. You can always ask for that.
Why are hospital beds so different from my bed at home?

Hospital beds are specially designed to help take care of you! They can be raised and lowered, the head part can tilt up so you can sit and eat or watch a show, and they have rails on the sides to keep you from rolling out. Some even have buttons you can push yourself! They might not be as cozy as your bed at home, but they're built to make your care easier.
I want my own bed. This bed is weird.

Hospital beds do feel pretty different, don't they? They make funny noises and move in strange ways. It's totally normal to miss your own cozy bed at home. One thing that might help is having your own pillow or blanket from home — your family can bring those for you. And even though the bed is different, the people around you are here to make sure you're safe and comfortable. If something about the bed bothers you, tell your nurse — they might be able to adjust it for you.
I'm scared to eat because I threw up before.

That makes total sense — nobody wants to throw up again, and it's smart to be cautious. Your nurse and doctor know about this and they'll tell you when it's a good time to try eating again. When you do try, they'll probably start you off with something really gentle, like small sips of water or crackers. You don't have to eat a big meal right away. Go at your own pace and let your care team know how your tummy is feeling. They're the experts at helping your tummy feel ready again.
I'm scared of needles. What will they do?

It's totally okay to feel scared of needles — lots of kids feel that way! The good news is that Children's Hospital has something called the Comfort Promise. That means they'll do everything they can to make needle time easier for you. They can put a special numbing cream on your skin so you barely feel anything. They'll also help you sit in a cozy position, and you can watch a video or play with a toy to keep your mind busy. You can always tell your nurse if you're feeling scared — they want to help!
What does a physiotherapist do?

A physiotherapist — sometimes called a physio — helps you with moving your body. If you had surgery or an injury, they'll teach you exercises and movements to help your muscles get strong again. They might also help you learn to walk with crutches or figure out the safest way to get in and out of a car. They're like a coach for your body!
What is a wheelchair and will I need one?

A wheelchair is a chair with wheels that helps people get around when walking is hard. You might use one if you're feeling tired, if your legs are sore, or if you're coming out of a procedure. There are wheelchairs at the hospital entrances, and a nurse or volunteer can help you get one. Not everyone needs a wheelchair — your care team will let you know. Getting pushed around in a wheelchair can actually be kind of fun, like a ride!
Someone in the hospital said they're a volunteer. What do volunteers do?

Volunteers are really kind people who come to Children's Hospital to help out without getting paid — they do it because they want to! You might see them at the information desks near the B1 entrance or B2 lobby, helping families find their way. Some volunteers help in playrooms, bring activity carts around, or help with special events. Guide volunteers are at the hospital from 8 in the morning to 3 in the afternoon on weekdays. They're some of the friendliest people you'll meet!
Will I have to come back to the hospital again?

That's a question your doctor is the best person to answer, because it depends on what's going on with your health. Some kids come to the hospital once and don't come back, and some kids come back for check-ups or treatments. But no matter what, the hospital isn't a scary place — it's a place that helps you. And if you do have to come back, you'll already know what to expect, which makes it much easier. Ask your doctor about the plan so you're not left wondering. Whatever happens, you'll handle it.
Someone put numbing cream on my skin before a needle. Why would a nurse do that?

Because your nurse wants the needle to hurt as little as possible! At Children's Hospital, they have something called the Comfort Promise. That means they try their very best to make every needle less painful and less scary. The numbing cream is called a topical anesthetic, and it makes your skin feel sleepy so you barely feel the poke. Your nurse might also help you sit in a comfy position or use toys and videos to distract you. They really do care about your comfort!
What if I need something from the store?

There are gift shops at the hospital where your family can buy things you might need. The pharmacy at B1-001 is open Monday to Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., and Victoria's Place is at the B1 entrance. Your nurse can point your family in the right direction.
Can a dog visit me in the hospital?

Children's Hospital has a special therapy dog program with dogs from St. John Ambulance. These therapy dogs are very well-trained and gentle, and they visit kids to help them feel happier and more relaxed. You can ask your nurse or care team if a therapy dog visit is coming up! Your own family pet usually can't visit, but in very special cases, the hospital might allow it with special permission. Ask your care team if you'd like to know more.
Who is the person who talked to my mom about how she's feeling?

That was probably a social worker. Social workers at Children's Hospital are here to help your whole family — not just you! They talk to moms, dads, and other family members about how they're feeling, and they can help with things like finding places to stay, figuring out tricky paperwork, or just being someone to talk to when things feel hard. It's their job to make sure your family is okay too.
A person let me play with a dog today! Who brought the dog?

How exciting! That was a therapy dog visit. Children's Hospital works with a group called St. John Ambulance to bring specially trained therapy dogs to visit kids. These dogs are super gentle and friendly, and spending time with them can make you feel happier and less worried. The person with the dog is a trained handler who makes sure the dog is safe and well-behaved. You can ask your care team if there's another therapy dog visit coming up!
What is the numbing cream for?

The numbing cream is part of something called the Comfort Promise at Children's Hospital. Before you get a needle, the nurse can put a special cream on your skin that makes it go a bit numb, so the poke hurts a lot less. It works kind of like magic — it tells the nerves in your skin to take a little nap! You can always ask for it before a needle procedure.
Why do I have to wash my hands so much?

Washing your hands is one of the best things you can do at the hospital! Germs are tiny things you can't see, and they can make people sick. At the hospital, you wash your hands or use the hand sanitizer gel before going into a room, when leaving a room, and before eating. This helps stop germs from getting to you or to other kids. Think of it like being a germ-fighting superhero — every time you wash your hands, you're protecting yourself and everyone around you!
Is there a playroom here?

Yes, there are some really cool spaces to play! The School-Age Activity Room on the sixth floor (B6-065) has crafts, board games, puzzles, and LEGO. It's open during the day, Monday through Saturday. There's also Ashley's Backyard (B6-259), which is a nature-themed playroom for younger kids to relax and play with a grown-up.
What does an X-ray machine do?

An X-ray machine takes pictures of the inside of your body — kind of like a camera, but instead of seeing your face, it can see your bones! It uses a special kind of light that you can't see or feel. You just have to hold very still for a few seconds while it takes the picture. It doesn't hurt at all. The picture helps your doctor see if anything inside needs attention.
It hurts and I don't like it.

I'm sorry you're hurting — that's really no fun at all. You're doing such a good job by telling someone about it. Your nurse and doctor need to know when you're in pain so they can help. Can you tell your nurse or your parent where it hurts and how much? Some kids use a number from 0 to 10, and some use faces that show how they feel. There are things your care team can do to help you feel more comfortable, so please always speak up when something hurts. You deserve to feel as good as possible.
I'm scared to be here at night.

Nighttime in a new place can feel a little spooky, and that's a really normal feeling. But you're in a safe place. Your nurses are right outside and they come in to check on you through the night — that's their job, to make sure you're comfortable and safe. If your mom or dad is staying, they'll be right beside you. You can also ask for a small light to be left on, or bring your favourite stuffed animal to cuddle. If you wake up and feel worried, it's always okay to press your call button.
There was a person who talked to me about going home. Who was that?

That was someone from your care team helping you get ready for discharge — which is the word for going home from the hospital! It could have been your nurse, a doctor, or a social worker. They want to make sure your family knows everything about your medicines, any follow-up visits, and how to take care of you at home. Going home is exciting, and your care team wants to make sure you're completely ready!
What is the red bracelet for?

If you have any allergies, you'll be given a special red bracelet. This bracelet tells everyone on your care team — nurses, doctors, and other helpers — about your allergies so they can keep you extra safe. It's like a little alert signal that everyone can see!
What's it like to have stitches?

If you need stitches, a doctor will use a special needle and thread to close up a cut so it can heal properly. Before they start, they'll numb the area so you don't feel the stitching — you might feel some pressure or tugging, but not sharp pain. The stitches look like tiny loops of thread in your skin. After a while, when the cut has healed, you'll come back or a nurse will take them out. Some stitches even dissolve on their own! If you're nervous about it, tell your care team and they can help you feel more comfortable.
My nurse has a red bracelet on my wrist. Did she put it there?

Yes, your nurse or another member of your care team put that red bracelet on you. A red bracelet is a special allergy bracelet. It tells every single person who helps take care of you that you have an allergy they need to know about. It's like a little signal flag that says 'Hey, be careful with this!' That way, no one accidentally gives you something that might make you feel bad. It's there to keep you safe!
What if I feel pain?

It's really important that you tell someone if you feel pain! The nurses and doctors at Children's Hospital really care about making sure you're comfortable. They might ask you to point to a face on a chart that shows how much it hurts — from a happy face to a really sad face. That helps them know the best way to help you. There are lots of ways they can help with pain, so always speak up. You're not being a bother — helping with pain is part of their job!
My friend at school is sick too. I hope they're okay.

That's really thoughtful of you to be thinking of your friend. It shows what a caring person you are. You're both in good hands — whether they're at a hospital or at home, there are people taking care of them just like people are taking care of you. When you're feeling better, you could make them a get-well card or call them to let them know you're thinking of them. Taking care of yourself right now is also a way of being a good friend, because you'll be there for them once you're feeling better too.
There's someone at the hospital who helped my dad find where to park. Who was that?

That was probably a volunteer or someone from the parking office! Children's Hospital has a parking garage called P8 off Baseline Road, and there are friendly people who help families figure out where to park, how to pay for their ticket, and how to get from the parking lot into the hospital. Guide volunteers near the entrances can also help with directions. Everyone works together to make sure families don't get lost!
The kid in the next bed was crying really loud. Are they okay?

It can be upsetting to hear another kid crying. You have a really caring heart for worrying about them. I can't tell you exactly what's going on with that child because their health information is private, just like yours is. But I can tell you that their nurses and doctors are taking really good care of them, just like your team is taking good care of you. Sometimes kids cry because they're scared or uncomfortable, and the hospital staff are great at helping with that.
Why does everyone keep washing their hands all the time?

Great observation! Everyone washes their hands so much because it's the number one best way to keep germs from spreading. In a hospital, keeping germs away is super important because some kids' bodies are working really hard to get better and germs could make that harder. When people wash their hands before coming into your room and when they leave, they're actually protecting YOU. You can help too by washing your hands before eating and after using the bathroom. Think of it like putting on invisible germ-fighting gloves!
What is a nurse practitioner?

A nurse practitioner is someone who is kind of like a mix between a nurse and a doctor. They've done lots of extra school and training, so they can do many of the same things a doctor does — like figuring out what's wrong and planning your care. They work really closely with your doctor and are another important member of your care team!
Can I bring family photos?

Yes! Bringing a few family pictures is a great idea — they can help your room feel more like home and make you feel less homesick. Just try not to bring too many things, because keeping your space tidy helps the nurses take good care of you.
Why do I have to wear this bracelet?

That bracelet is your special hospital armband! It has your name, your birthday, and a barcode on it. Every time a nurse or doctor gives you medicine or does a test, they check your bracelet to make sure they're helping the right person. It's one of the ways the hospital keeps you safe.
What does an occupational therapist do?

An occupational therapist — sometimes called an OT — helps you learn or re-learn everyday things like getting dressed, eating, writing, or playing. If your body needs some extra help doing the things you normally do, the OT comes up with fun ways to practise and get better at them. They're really creative and good at making activities that feel more like play than work!
I don't like when people I don't know touch me.

That's a completely reasonable feeling, and it's really important that you said it out loud. Your body is yours, and it's okay to feel uncomfortable when someone you don't know touches you. In the hospital, the doctors and nurses do need to examine you sometimes, but they should always explain what they're going to do first and ask if you're ready. If someone doesn't do that, you or your parent can remind them. You can also ask to have your parent right next to you during any exam. Speaking up about what makes you uncomfortable is always the right thing to do.
Why is the hospital so big?

Great question! Children's Hospital is big because it has lots of different rooms for lots of different things. There are rooms where doctors check on kids, rooms with special machines that can take pictures of the inside of your body, rooms where families can rest, and even playrooms! It's kind of like a small city — everything kids and their families need is all in one building so nobody has to go far.
Who is the security guard at the door?

That's a security guard, and their job is to keep everyone in the hospital safe — including you! At Children's Hospital, security guards are at the entrances, especially after 8:30 at night when the main doors are locked. They also walk around the hospital to check that everything is okay. If your family ever needs someone to walk them to their car or to the Ronald McDonald House, the security team can help with that too. They're like the hospital's protectors!
What do I do at the hospital if I get bored?

There are lots of things to do if you get bored! You can visit the activity rooms on the sixth floor for crafts and games, try the SMILE Room with its cool lights and music, ask about art therapy or music therapy, or see if Ollie the Clown is visiting. You can also bring your own toys, books, colouring supplies, or a tablet from home. There's free TV and you can use your family's streaming services. And the Heroes' Circle program teaches fun breathing and martial arts moves!
Why do I need to tell the nurse when I go to the bathroom?

Sometimes the doctors need to keep track of how your body is working, and going to the bathroom is one of the clues! It helps them know if you're drinking enough water and if your body is doing its job properly. It might feel a little weird to talk about, but it's totally normal in a hospital. Your nurse has heard it all before, so don't be shy!
What if I get lost in the hospital?

If you ever feel lost, look for an Information Desk — they're open from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. on weekdays, and noon to 4:00 p.m. on weekends. You can also ask any staff member or volunteer wearing a hospital badge. There are friendly guide volunteers at the B1 entrance and B2 lobby on weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. who love to help!
What is the family lounge?

The Culliton Family Lounge is a comfy space on the sixth floor in room B6-110 where you can hang out with your family or friends and take a break from your hospital room. It's also used for special group events and family coffee hours. It's a nice place to relax, chat, or just spend time together in a different spot. If you're staying on the B6 inpatient unit, you're welcome to use it!
Can I bring books from home?

Yes! Bringing books from home is a great idea. They can help you feel more comfortable and give you something fun to do. Just make sure they're clean, and try not to share them with other patients. The Paediatric Family Resource Centre on the 1st floor of Zone B also has information you can look at.
Why are the bed rails up?

The rails on the sides of your bed are there to keep you safe, like a little fence! When you're sleeping or resting, the rails make sure you don't accidentally roll out of bed. Your grown-up or nurse will put them up when you're lying down. When you want to get out of bed, just ask for help and someone will lower the rail for you. If you're in a crib, the sides stay up for the same reason — to keep you safe and snug!
I had an accident in my bed. I'm embarrassed.

Please don't be embarrassed — this happens to a lot of kids in the hospital, way more than you'd think. Your body is going through a lot right now, and sometimes accidents just happen. The nurses are completely used to it and they won't judge you or make you feel bad at all. They'll help you get cleaned up and get fresh sheets really quickly. It's just part of being in the hospital, and there's nothing to feel ashamed about. You're handling a lot, and you're doing a great job.
What is that beeping machine next to my bed?

That beeping machine is called a monitor, and it's like a helper that watches over you! It keeps track of things like how fast your heart is beating and how much oxygen is in your blood. The beeping sounds usually mean everything is working fine — it's just the machine doing its job. Sometimes it beeps a little louder if something moves or gets loose, like the clip on your finger. A nurse will always come check if the beeping changes, so you don't need to worry about it!
Why does my room have a curtain?

The curtain is there to give you privacy! If you're sharing a room with another patient, or when a nurse needs to check on you, the curtain can be pulled closed so you have your own private space. It's like a soft, movable wall. If you ever want your curtain open or closed, just ask!
What happens when the nurse takes my temperature with an ear thermometer?

The nurse will gently put a small probe into your ear — it doesn't go in very far, just a tiny bit. You'll hear a little beep after a second or two, and that's it! The thermometer reads how warm you are from inside your ear. It doesn't hurt, but it might feel a little tickly. Each time the nurse uses it, they put a brand new clean cover on the tip. It's one of the quickest check-ups the nurse does!
Why does blood need to be tested?

Your blood carries lots of important information about how your body is doing. When the doctor takes a little bit of blood to test, they're looking at things like how many red and white blood cells you have and how your body is working on the inside. It helps them understand the best way to help you feel better. The test itself is quick — just a small poke!
What is hand sanitizer and why is it everywhere?

You'll see little bottles and dispensers of hand sanitizer all over the hospital — they're everywhere! It's a special gel you rub on your hands to get rid of germs. The hospital calls it ABHR, which stands for alcohol-based hand rub. Everyone uses it — doctors, nurses, your family, and you too! You should clean your hands when you go into a room, when you leave a room, and before you eat. It helps keep germs from spreading so everyone stays healthier.
Can I watch TV? I want to forget I'm here.

Wanting to take your mind off things is totally understandable! Children's Hospital has a patient entertainment site where you can watch live TV for free or use your own streaming accounts if you have them. Watching your favourite show can be a great way to relax and feel a little more normal. You could also ask about games, crafts, or a visit from a Child Life Specialist. Taking breaks from thinking about hospital stuff is healthy — you don't have to be focused on being a patient every minute!
Why do they have hand sanitizer at every door?

There are hand sanitizer dispensers at every door because clean hands are the number one way to stop germs from spreading in the hospital! Every person — doctors, nurses, visitors, and kids — should clean their hands when going in and out of rooms. The hospital uses alcohol-based hand rub, and it only takes about 20 seconds to rub it all over your hands. Think of each dispenser as a tiny germ-fighting station, and you're the hero who uses it!
Can I go to the playroom? I need to do something fun.

Wanting to do something fun is a great sign! Children's Hospital has some really cool spaces for kids. There's a School-Age Activity Room on the sixth floor with crafts, board games, puzzles, and LEGO. There's also Ashley's Backyard, which is a nature-themed playroom for younger kids. Ask your nurse if you're allowed to leave your room right now — sometimes you need permission depending on your care plan. If you can't go yet, a Child Life Specialist might be able to bring some activities to your room. Fun is important medicine too!
Why do people keep asking me my name and birthday?

I know it might feel a bit silly to keep saying it over and over! But every time someone asks your name and birthday, they're checking your armband to make sure you're getting exactly the right care. It's one of the most important safety rules in the hospital. Think of it like a secret password — it keeps you safe!
What is the activity room?

The School-Age Activity Room is in room B6-065 on the sixth floor, and it's full of fun things to do! You can make crafts, play board games, put puzzles together, and build with LEGO. It's open during the day from Monday to Saturday. Sometimes the Child Life staff and volunteers plan special activities and events there too! You and your family can use the room on your own, or you can join in when there's a planned activity. Just ask your nurse when it's a good time to visit.
Someone gave me a schedule of when a dog would visit. Who made that schedule?

The therapy dog visits at Children's Hospital are organized through a program with St. John Ambulance. Your care team or a Child Life Specialist probably shared that schedule with you. The visits are planned ahead of time so kids can look forward to them. If you want to know when the next visit is happening on your unit, just ask your nurse — they'll know if one is coming up!
Someone brought me beads and said I earn them. Who was that?

That was probably a Child Life Specialist telling you about the Bravery Beads program! Bravery Beads is a special program at Children's Hospital where each bead stands for something you've been through — like a test, a treatment, or a brave moment. Over time, you collect beads that tell YOUR story. It's totally up to you if you want to join — it's voluntary. But a lot of kids think it's really cool to see how many beads they earn. Each one is proof of how brave you are!
Where is the hospital?

Children's Hospital is at 800 Commissioners Road East in London, Ontario. It's part of a bigger place called the Victoria Hospital site, and the children's part is in an area called Zone B. If your family is driving here, the closest parking is Parking Lot 8, which is a parking garage you can get to from Baseline Road.
I'm getting a cast. Does it hurt?

Getting a cast put on actually doesn't hurt! The material they wrap around your arm or leg starts off wet and warm, and then it gets hard as it dries. It might feel a little weird, but it shouldn't be painful. The cast is like a super-strong shield that protects your bone while it heals. You might even get to pick a colour! If anything does feel uncomfortable or too tight after it's on, make sure you tell your nurse or doctor right away so they can fix it.
What if my mom needs to leave for a bit?

It's okay if your mom needs to step away for a little while. She just needs to let the nurse know so they can keep an extra close eye on you. Before she goes, she'll make sure the rails on your bed or crib are up and that only safe things are within your reach. She can also ask security to walk her to her car if it's dark outside by calling extension 52281.
That machine looks scary. What does it do?

I get why it might look a little scary — hospital machines can look big and confusing! But most of them are just there to help keep an eye on you and make sure you're doing well. They're kind of like friendly robots. If there's a machine near your bed that's making you nervous, ask your nurse or a Child Life Specialist to explain what it does. Once you know what it's for, it usually feels a lot less scary. You're being so brave just for asking about it!
Do I have to stay in my room the whole time?

Not always! Depending on how you're feeling and what your doctors say, you might be able to visit the playrooms, family spaces, or other areas. But always check with your nurse first — sometimes there are rules about staying in your room, especially if you need extra germ protection.
Who is the person who talked about what I eat at the hospital cafeteria?

If someone was helping your family find food in the hospital, it might have been your nurse, a volunteer, or the person working at the Tim Hortons spot called 'On the Go' on the second floor of Zone B. That's the closest place to buy food, and it's open on weekdays from 6:30 in the morning to 8 at night. There are also vending machines near the elevators in Zone B on the first and third floors. Your care team can help you find the best food options!
Can I bring my LEGO to the hospital?

Yes, you can bring LEGO from home! Just try not to bring too many pieces, because keeping your room tidy helps the nurses take care of you. Make sure your LEGO pieces are clean, and remember not to share them with other kids in the hospital. There's also LEGO in the School-Age Activity Room if you want even more building fun!
Can my family eat in my room?

Your family can be with you during your meals! If they want to get their own food, there's Tim Hortons on the second floor of Zone B (open weekdays 6:30 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.) and vending machines on the 1st and 3rd floors of Zone B near the elevators. They can also store food in the family fridge.
There's a lady who comes in and plays guitar and sings. Who is she?

She's a music therapist! Children's Hospital has a real music therapist who uses songs and instruments to help kids feel better. Music therapy can actually help with things like feeling less pain or being less worried. The cool part is you don't need to know how to play any instruments or be a good singer to join in — anyone can take part. If you liked her visit, you can ask your nurse if the music therapist can come back again!
Can I do arts and crafts here?

You sure can! The School-Age Activity Room on the sixth floor (B6-065) has crafts you can do, and Child Life staff and volunteers plan special art activities too. There's also an Art Therapy program that helps kids express their feelings through art. Ask your nurse or a Child Life Specialist about what's available!
Why do I have to stay in my room sometimes?

Sometimes your doctor needs you to stay in your room because of something called infection precautions. It might mean that your body needs extra protection from germs, or that you have germs that shouldn't spread to other kids. It can feel boring, but the nurses will make sure you have things to do, and people like Child Life Specialists might visit you with activities. It's all about keeping everyone safe!
What is that pole with the bag hanging on it?

That's called an IV pole! The bag hanging on it is filled with special fluid or medicine that drips slowly through a tube and into your IV. The pole has wheels on the bottom so you can roll it along with you if you need to get up and walk around. Some kids even give their IV pole a name — you can too if you want!
Why do I have to stay in bed?

Sometimes the doctors and nurses want you to stay in bed so your body can rest and get better. It also helps them keep an eye on you and make sure all the machines and tubes are working just right. But staying in bed doesn't mean you can't have fun! You can play with toys, read books, watch shows, or do crafts right from your bed. And when it's safe, your nurse might let you get up and walk around or visit one of the playrooms.
Will the IV hurt?

When the IV first goes in, there's a little poke from a small needle. But the good news is the nurses at Children's Hospital use the Comfort Promise! That means they can put numbing cream on your skin first so you barely feel the poke. They'll also help you sit in a cozy position, and you can watch something fun or play with a toy while it happens. Once the IV is in, the needle comes out, and the soft tube that stays doesn't hurt. If something ever feels uncomfortable, just tell your nurse right away.
Will the blood test hurt a lot?

It's really normal to worry about that. Most kids say it feels like a quick little pinch, and then it's over before they know it. The nurses here are really good at making it as easy as possible — they can put numbing cream on your arm first so it doesn't sting, and they might let you blow bubbles or watch something on a screen to keep your mind busy. If you're feeling scared, that's completely okay. Talk to your nurse or your parent and they'll help you feel ready.
I don't want to take my medicine. It tastes yucky.

Some medicine really does taste pretty yucky — you're not wrong about that! But your medicine is working hard to help your body feel better, even if it doesn't taste great. You can ask your nurse if there's a way to make it easier — sometimes medicine can be mixed with juice or given in a different way. Taking a sip of something you like right after can help wash the taste away too. You're doing an awesome job, and every time you take your medicine, you're one step closer to feeling better!
What does a medical student do here?

A medical student is someone who already graduated from regular university and is now in medical school learning how to be a doctor. At Children's Hospital, medical students get to practise by helping take care of kids like you — but they always have a real doctor or resident watching over them. They might listen to your heart, ask you questions, or help with your care plan. You're actually teaching them while they're helping you — how cool is that?
What does the hand sanitizer do?

The hand sanitizer — also called alcohol-based hand rub — kills the germs on your hands really quickly. It's the best way to clean your hands when they don't look dirty. You'll see dispensers all around the hospital, and everyone — doctors, nurses, visitors, and you — should use them before entering and leaving patient rooms!
The nurses are really nice but I'm just tired of being here.

Being tired of the hospital is one of the most common feelings there is. Even when everyone is kind and caring, it doesn't change the fact that you want to be home living your regular life. That tiredness is completely valid. Every day might feel long, but you're getting through each one, and that takes real strength. Try to find one small good thing each day — a yummy snack, a visitor, a funny show — and hold onto it. And keep talking to your care team about how you're feeling. They care about your mood, not just your body.
What is the family fridge for?

The family fridge is where your family can store food they bring from home. It even has a freezer! Just make sure to write your name and the date on everything. The hospital isn't responsible if someone accidentally takes your food, so labels really help. Check with your care team before eating anything that's brought in.
Why do some rooms have signs on the door?

Sometimes you might see a colourful sign on a door when you're walking around the hospital. Those signs are there to let people know about special rules for that room. It might mean the person inside needs extra germ protection. The sign might say that visitors need to wear gloves, a gown, or a mask before going in. If you see a sign like that, just check with a nurse before you go in. It's all about keeping everyone safe and healthy!
Why do I have to wear slip-proof socks?

The hospital floors can be really smooth and slippery, so wearing slip-proof socks — the kind with little grippy dots on the bottom — helps make sure you don't slide or fall. Falls can happen easily, especially if you've been lying down for a while and feel a little wobbly. Your nurse might remind you to put on your non-slip socks or slippers every time you get out of bed. It's a simple thing that helps keep you safe!
Who is the person who helped me learn to eat differently after my surgery?

That could have been a dietitian or a speech therapist. A dietitian helps figure out which foods are best for you after surgery, especially if your tummy or body needs something different for a while. A speech therapist might help if you're having trouble swallowing or eating safely. They both work together with your doctor and nurse to make sure you're eating in a way that helps your body heal. If eating feels tricky, tell your care team!
What is that sign on the door of some rooms?

Sometimes a room has a special sign because the patient inside needs extra protection from germs, or because they have germs that shouldn't spread to others. The sign tells visitors to check with the nurses before going in. You might need to wear gloves, a gown, or a mask before entering. It's not scary — it's just another way the hospital keeps everyone safe!
I saw a dog with a special vest in the hallway. Whose dog is that?

That's a therapy dog! The dog wears a special vest to show that it's working. Children's Hospital partners with St. John Ambulance to bring trained therapy dogs to visit kids. The handler — the person walking with the dog — makes sure the dog is gentle and safe. Therapy dogs can make you feel happier and less stressed. Family pets aren't allowed in the hospital, but therapy dogs are special because they're trained to visit patients. Ask your care team if a therapy dog visit is coming to your unit!
Everyone is so nice but I still don't want to be here.

That makes perfect sense — the people can be wonderful, but the hospital is still not where you'd choose to be. You can appreciate the nice nurses and doctors while also wishing you were home in your own bed. Both feelings can be true at the same time. The people here are nice because they genuinely care about kids like you, and they understand that you'd rather be somewhere else. Just keep focusing on getting better, and you'll be out of here before you know it.
Why do some doors have codes on them?

Some areas of the hospital have special door codes to keep patients extra safe. For example, the B6 inpatient unit is a locked unit, and when you're admitted, you'll get a secret code to use. It's kind of like a password! It makes sure only people who belong on that floor can get in, which helps keep everyone secure.
Is there a playroom I can go to?

Yes! Children's Hospital has some awesome spaces for playing. There's Ashley's Backyard in room B6-259 — it's a nature-themed playroom for younger kids and their families. There's also the School-Age Activity Room in B6-065 where you can do crafts, play board games, work on puzzles, and build with LEGO. Child Life staff and volunteers set up fun activities there too. Ask your nurse if you're allowed to visit!
Why can't I bring flowers to someone?

Some parts of the hospital don't allow flowers because certain plants can carry germs or cause allergies for patients who are very sensitive. There's also a plant called a poinsettia that's never allowed because it contains stuff similar to latex, which some people are really allergic to. If you want to cheer someone up, cards, drawings, or mylar balloons are great alternatives!
There's a person who keeps asking me to move my arms and legs. Who are they?

That's probably a physiotherapist! A physiotherapist is someone who knows all about how your body moves. They might ask you to stretch, walk, or do little exercises to help your body get stronger or feel better. They're kind of like a coach for your muscles and bones. Everything they ask you to do is to help your body heal, even if it seems a little silly sometimes!
Can someone walk my mom to the car at night?

Yes! If your mom needs to go to her car when it's dark, she can call the Security team at extension 52281 and they'll send someone to walk with her. They can also walk her to the Ronald McDonald House. It's there to help everyone feel safe.
Where is the garden?

There's a beautiful garden called Alex's Butterfly Garden on Level 2 of Zone D. It's a quiet, peaceful outdoor space with benches and a water fountain. Kids, families, and staff can all go there to enjoy some fresh air and quiet time.
There was a person in the emergency room who checked if I had anything dangerous. Who was that?

That was a security guard! At the Emergency Department at Children's Hospital, everyone walks through a special system that checks for things that could be dangerous, like weapons. It's really quick — you don't have to stop or take anything out of your pockets. The security guard is there to help if the machine beeps. It's the same idea as airport security — it's there to make sure everyone inside is safe. The guards are friendly and happy to explain what's happening if you're curious.
Why does the nurse keep asking me my name?

I know it might seem silly when they already know you, but checking your name and birthday is one of the most important safety rules in the hospital. They do it before giving medicine, doing tests, or taking you somewhere — it's how they make double sure everything is right. You're helping keep yourself safe every time you answer!
Why does everything need to be so clean?

When you're at home, a few germs are no big deal because your body is strong enough to fight them off. But in a hospital, many kids are already using their body's energy to get better, so they can't fight off extra germs as easily. That's why the hospital cleans everything so carefully and asks everyone to wash their hands a lot — it gives every kid the best chance of getting better faster!
Someone told my mom about a house she can stay at near the hospital. Who was that?

That was probably a social worker or another member of your care team. They were most likely talking about the Ronald McDonald House! It's a special place near Children's Hospital where families who live far away from London can stay while their child is in the hospital. It's like a home away from home. If your family needs a place to stay, your care team can help figure out the best option.
What should I wear home from the hospital?
Your parents should bring you a comfy set of clothes for going home! Make sure they bring shoes too. When you find out your discharge day, having your clothes ready will make everything go smoothly.
What is a Child Life Specialist?

A Child Life Specialist is someone whose whole job is to help kids feel better about being in the hospital! They're experts at helping kids understand what's happening, preparing you for things like tests or procedures, and helping you cope through play and fun activities. They can bring you toys, help with crafts, and explain things in ways that make sense. If you're feeling worried about something, a Child Life Specialist is a great person to talk to!
Who is the person who put a secret code on the door for my mom?

That was most likely your nurse on the B6 inpatient unit! That floor is a locked unit, which means the door needs a special code to open. When you're admitted there, your nurse gives your parent or caregiver a confidential code — kind of like a secret password — so they can get in and out. It's locked to keep all the kids on that floor extra safe. Only the people who are supposed to be there know the code!
What is that clip thing they put on my finger?

That little clip is called a pulse oximeter, but you can think of it as a finger light! It clips gently onto your finger and shines a tiny red light through your skin. It's checking how much oxygen is in your blood — oxygen is the stuff you breathe in that your body needs. It doesn't hurt at all, and some kids think the glowing red light looks pretty cool! The nurse just needs to make sure your body is getting all the oxygen it needs.
Why is this happening to me?

That's such a big question, and it's totally okay to wonder that. Getting sick or hurt isn't something you caused — it's not your fault at all. Sometimes bodies just need a little extra help. The important thing is that you're in a place full of people who really care about you and know how to help. If you're feeling sad or frustrated, you can talk to your nurse, your parent, or a Child Life Specialist. They're here to listen and to help you through this.
My nurse introduced me to a new nurse at her bedside. Why?

That's called a bedside shift change report! When one nurse's shift is ending and a new nurse is starting, they come to your bedside together to talk about how you're doing. They go over your care plan, do some safety checks, and make sure the new nurse knows everything important about you. Your parent or caregiver can listen in and even ask questions. It usually only takes about three to five minutes, and it helps make sure nothing important gets missed!
I'm trying to be brave but I keep crying.

You know what? Crying and being brave can happen at the same time. Being brave doesn't mean you never feel scared or sad — it means you keep going even when things are hard. And that's exactly what you're doing! Every single person who works here has seen kids cry, and they all think those kids are brave too. So let those tears out if you need to. And if you want to talk about what's making you upset, your nurse, your parent, or a Child Life Specialist would love to listen.
What is a thermometer doing in my ear?

An ear thermometer is a quick way to check your temperature — that means how warm your body is. It works by reading the heat coming from inside your ear. It only takes a second and it doesn't hurt! It might feel a little tickly. Your nurse checks your temperature to make sure your body is doing okay.
What if I need a toothbrush?

If you forgot your toothbrush or need other things like deodorant or shampoo, you can get them at the Paediatric Family Resource Centre, the Ronald McDonald Room, or one of the gift shops in the hospital. Just ask your nurse where to find them!
Can I share my toys with the kid in the next bed?

It's really nice that you want to share, but in the hospital we don't share toys or personal items between patients. This is to stop germs from spreading. Your toys stay with you, and the other kid has their own things. If you want to play together, a nurse or Child Life Specialist can help figure out a safe way to have fun!
How can I tell my nurse something?

You can always talk to your nurse directly, or press the call button near your bed. During bedside shift changes, which happen in the morning and evening, you and your parent are invited to share anything important. Never be afraid to speak up — the nurses want to hear from you!
Why can't I bring balloons to the hospital?

Some kinds of balloons — the stretchy ones made of latex — aren't allowed at Children's Hospital. That's because some people are really allergic to latex, and being near those balloons could make them very sick. But here's the thing — you can still bring the shiny foil balloons! Those are safe for everyone. So if someone wants to bring you a get-well balloon, just remind them to get the foil kind.
What happens when I first get to the hospital?

When you first arrive at Children's Hospital, you'll come in through the big main entrance in the B Tower. A friendly person at a desk might say hello! Then you and your grown-up will go up to the second floor to a place called Patient Registration. That's where they write down your name and make sure everything is ready for your visit. It's kind of like checking in at a hotel — but instead of getting a room key, you'll get a special bracelet to wear on your wrist!
What is the Ronald McDonald House?

Ronald McDonald House is a special home away from home for families who have a child in the hospital. If your family lives far from London, they can stay there instead of a hotel. It's close to the hospital so they can visit you easily. It has bedrooms, a kitchen, and common areas where families can relax. Your care team can help your family find out if they can stay there.
Can my mom stay with me overnight?

Yes! Most patient rooms have a spot where a parent or caregiver can sleep right next to you. There will be clean sheets, pillows, and blankets for them. Your mom just needs to stay in your room during the nighttime hours — between 8:00 p.m. and 8:00 a.m. — and let the nurses know she's there.
What is a waiting room like?

A waiting room is a big room with chairs where families sit and wait until it's their turn to see the doctor or have a test done. You might see other kids and families there too. There are usually things to look at or read, and you can bring your own books, toys, or a tablet to keep busy. Sometimes the wait can feel long, but your grown-up will be right there with you. When it's your turn, someone will call your name and take you to where you need to go.
What is a nebulizer?

A nebulizer is a machine that turns liquid medicine into a fine mist so you can breathe it right into your lungs. You wear a little mask over your nose and mouth, or sometimes just use a mouthpiece, and breathe normally while the mist comes out. The machine makes a quiet humming sound, and the mist might feel cool or wet on your face. It doesn't hurt at all! You just sit and breathe for about 10 to 15 minutes while the medicine goes in. You can watch TV or read a book while it's working.
Why can't I eat before my test?

Some tests and procedures need your tummy to be completely empty to work properly and to keep you safe. If there's food in your stomach, it could cause problems during certain procedures. I know being hungry isn't fun at all, but your nurse will let you know the second you're allowed to eat again! It's one of those things that's worth the wait.
What time is lunch?

Lunch arrives between 11:45 a.m. and 12:45 p.m. You'll get a menu form on your breakfast tray so you can pick what you'd like to eat the next day — kind of like ordering from a restaurant! If you have a question about what foods you can have, your nurse can help.
There's a person who helped my mom fill out papers. Who are they?

That person might work at Patient Registration, or they could be someone from the Paediatric Family Resource Centre. Patient Registration is where families check in when they first arrive — it's on the second floor of Zone B. The Family Resource Centre on the first floor of Zone B also helps families with forms and paperwork. Both of these helpers are there to make the confusing stuff easier for your family!
Am I going to fail because I'm missing school?

It's really smart of you to think about school, but try not to worry too much about that right now. Your most important job is to rest and get better. Your parents can talk to your teacher about what you're missing, and teachers are usually really understanding when a student is in the hospital. There are people at the hospital who can help with that too. Right now, your health comes first, and you can catch up on schoolwork when you're ready. You're not going to fall behind just because your body needs some time to heal.
Am I in trouble? Is that why I'm here?

Oh no, you are absolutely not in trouble! The hospital is not a place where people go because they did something wrong. You're here because your body needs some help, and that is not your fault at all. The doctors, nurses, and everyone here are on your team — they all like kids and they chose this job because they want to help children feel better. You haven't done anything wrong, okay? You're being really brave just by being here.
Why can't the hospital be more like home?

I wish it could be more like home for you too. The hospital has to be set up in a certain way so doctors and nurses can do their jobs and keep everyone safe, but that doesn't mean you can't bring home to the hospital a little bit. Your family can bring your favourite blanket, pictures, books, and comfy clothes. You can keep some of your home routines, like what time you brush your teeth or what you like to do before bed. Your nurses want you to feel as comfortable as possible, so let them know what would help!
Can I use the supply cart in the hallway?

The supply carts in the hallway are for the hospital staff to use. Visitors and patients shouldn't touch the things on the carts. If you need something, just ask your nurse and they'll get it for you!
I have a test tomorrow and I can't sleep.

It's really hard to sleep when you're nervous about something the next day. Your brain keeps thinking about it, right? That's so normal. Try taking some slow, deep breaths — breathe in through your nose like you're smelling a flower, and out through your mouth like you're blowing out birthday candles. You could also ask your parent to read you a story or play some quiet music. And remember, your care team will explain everything before the test happens. If you're still really worried, it's okay to let your nurse know.
What do I do if the machines start beeping a lot?

If the machines near your bed start beeping more than usual, don't worry! Often the beeping just means something small happened — like the clip on your finger moved or a tube shifted a tiny bit.
