A nurse will come check on it. You don't have to fix anything yourself. If a nurse doesn't come right away, you can press your call button and let them know. The machines are there to help, and the beeping is their way of telling the nurses to come take a look.
Someone asked me to blow into a tube. Who was that person?

That was probably a respiratory therapist or a nurse doing a breathing test! Respiratory therapists are experts on lungs and breathing. Blowing into a tube helps them learn how well your lungs are working. It might feel silly, but the information from that puff of air tells your care team a lot! If you're curious about what the results mean, your care team can explain it in a way that makes sense to you.
Where do I go when I first get to the hospital?

When you arrive, you'll go to Patient Registration on the second floor of Zone B, which is above the main entrance. That's where they'll get you checked in. If you need help finding it, there are guide volunteers at the B1 entrance and B2 lobby on weekdays who can show you the way!
Can I bring snacks from home?

That depends! Before eating anything, you should always check with your nurse first because some kids are on special diets or need to avoid eating before procedures. If your care team says it's okay, your family can keep some personal snacks in the family fridge — just make sure they're labelled with your name and the date! There are also pantries on the B6 unit with drinks and light snacks for patients.
Why do I have to wash my hands so much?

Great question! Washing your hands is the number one best way to stop germs from spreading around the hospital. You should wash them when you go into a patient room, when you leave, and at the end of a visit. You can use soap and water or the hand sanitizer dispensers you'll see around the hospital.
Why do some people wear masks in the hospital?

People wear masks at Children's Hospital to keep germs from spreading. Masks help protect you, other patients, and the staff. Some people wear masks all the time, and sometimes you might see people wearing extra things like gloves and gowns when they come into your room. If there's a special sign on your door, it might mean extra germ-fighting steps are needed. Hospital masks are available right at the entrance for anyone who needs one. It's one of the ways the hospital keeps everyone healthy!
Somebody came and talked about what foods I can eat. Who was that?

That was probably a dietitian! A dietitian is a food expert who's part of your care team. They know all about which foods are best for your body, especially when you're in the hospital. They work with your doctor to make sure you're eating the right things to help you feel better. If you have allergies or there are foods you can't eat for religious reasons, the dietitian helps with that too. If you have questions about your meals, you can always ask!
The exercises hurt and I don't want to do them.

I hear you — exercises that make you sore are no fun at all. It's okay to say that. But those exercises are actually helping your body get stronger so you can get back to doing the things you love. Think of it like training for your favourite sport. Your physiotherapist can help adjust things if they're too painful, so make sure you tell them exactly how it feels. You can also take breaks and go at your own pace. Every little bit of effort counts, and your body will thank you later. You're doing awesome.
Will I look different after my surgery?

That's a really good question and it's totally natural to wonder about it. The answer depends on what kind of surgery you're having, so the very best person to ask is your doctor. They can explain exactly what to expect. Many surgeries don't change how you look at all, and even if there is a small scar, it usually gets smaller and lighter over time. Your doctor will be honest with you. And no matter what, you'll still be YOU — the same awesome person, inside and out.
My dad talked to someone about staying at a special house nearby. What house?

Your dad was probably hearing about the Ronald McDonald House! It's a special place right near Children's Hospital where families who live far from London, Ontario, can stay while their kid is in the hospital. It feels more like a real home than a hotel. There's also a Ronald McDonald Family Room inside the hospital. Your care team can help your dad figure out if your family can stay there and how to get set up.
My nurse helped me feel better when I was crying. I want to say thank you.

That's so wonderful that you want to thank your nurse! You could tell them directly — nurses love hearing that they made a difference. You could also draw them a picture or write a little thank-you note. There's even a way for your family to officially recognize a team member through the hospital's Great Moments program — your parent can fill out a form on the website to let the hospital know how special that nurse is. What a kind and thoughtful thing for you to want to do. That nurse is lucky to have a patient like you!
Why are there hand sanitizer dispensers everywhere?

The hospital puts hand sanitizer all over the place to make it super easy for everyone to clean their hands — doctors, nurses, patients, and visitors. Clean hands are the number one way to stop germs from spreading! The sanitizer has special alcohol in it that kills germs in just a few seconds. Try to use it every time you go in or out of a room, and always before eating.
Is there a clown at the hospital?

Yes! There's a really fun therapeutic clown named Ollie! Ollie visits kids in the hospital to bring laughter, play, and fun. A therapeutic clown is specially trained to help kids feel happy and more normal during their hospital stay. Ollie knows how to be gentle and funny in just the right way. If Ollie stops by your room, get ready for some giggles! And if you're feeling shy, that's okay too — Ollie understands.
What if I spill something in my room?

Accidents happen! If you spill something, let your nurse know. The cleaning staff will take care of it to make sure the floor doesn't get slippery. Keeping the floor clean and dry is important to prevent falls.
Why is the hospital so big?

Children's Hospital is part of a really big place called Victoria Hospital in London, Ontario. It's big because it has lots of different areas where different kinds of care happen. The hospital uses letters and numbers to organize everything — like Zone B and Zone D. Your room number even tells you which zone and floor you're on! For example, room B2-503 means Zone B, second floor, room 503. If you ever get confused, there are helpers at the information desks and a cool app called MazeMap that works like a map for the hospital.
Someone talked to my mom about money stuff. Who was that?

That was probably a social worker. Social workers at Children's Hospital can help families figure out money things — like finding financial help, filling out applications for support, or understanding hospital bills. The hospital also has a Business Office in Zone D on the third floor if your family has questions about charges for things not covered by OHIP, like certain supplies. Your care team wants to make sure your family isn't stressed about money on top of everything else.
Why can't I get out of bed by myself?

Your nurse wants to make sure you don't slip or fall, especially if you're feeling a little wobbly from being in bed or from medicine. The floors can be slippery sometimes too. Before you get up, just press your call button or ask a grown-up to let your nurse know. They might ask you to wear special non-slip socks to help keep you safe. It's all about keeping you from getting a boo-boo!
Why does someone walk into my room without knocking at night?

That's one of your nurses doing a nighttime check! During your whole stay, a nurse will come by regularly — even at night — to make sure you're safe and comfortable. They try to be very quiet so they don't wake you up. It's part of how they take good care of you around the clock.
I have a bandage on my face. What if kids laugh at me?

I understand why that worries you. But here at Children's Hospital, lots of kids have bandages, casts, and other things — it's totally normal here, and nobody thinks it's funny. Your bandage is actually a sign that you're healing, like a badge of courage. When you go back to school, most kids will probably think it's cool and want to hear your story. And real friends won't laugh — they'll be glad you're okay. If someone ever does say something unkind, you can talk to a grown-up about it. But I think you might be surprised by how nice people are.
I miss my sister. We do everything together.

Being apart from your sister when you're used to doing everything together must feel really strange. She probably misses you just as much! You can keep in touch by calling her on the patient phone or video chatting if you have a phone or tablet. Maybe you could both draw pictures for each other, or she could write you a letter to read. Your parent can help set up a special time for you two to talk. And the faster you focus on getting better, the sooner you'll be back together doing all your favourite things.
Why do some people in the hospital wear different coloured clothes?

Great eye! Different coloured scrubs sometimes help you tell what someone's job is. Some hospitals give nurses one colour, doctors another, and other team members another. It's kind of like how different sports teams have different jerseys — it helps everyone know who's who. If you're curious about someone's role, you can always ask them!
I saw someone pushing a cart with cleaning stuff. Who is that?

That's a member of the housekeeping or environmental services team! Their job is super important — they keep the hospital clean and germ-free so that everyone stays as healthy as possible. They clean patient rooms, hallways, and all the spaces you use. Keeping things clean is one of the biggest ways the hospital stops germs from spreading. They're like the hospital's germ-fighting heroes!
Can someone pray at the hospital?

Yes! There's a special place called the Sanctuary on the 3rd floor of Zone C (room C3-402). It's open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, and everyone is welcome. It's a quiet space for praying, thinking, or just having a peaceful moment. If your family would like to talk to a Spiritual Care Specialist, your nurse can help.
Can I walk around the hospital?

You might be able to, depending on how you're feeling and what your care team says. Some kids need to stay in their room or bed, especially if there are infection control rules. Always ask your nurse before going for a walk, and make sure you wear non-slip socks or shoes so you don't slip!
Can I do crafts at the hospital?

Yes! The School-Age Activity Room on the sixth floor (room B6-065) has all kinds of crafts for you. You might get to paint, make things with paper, build with LEGO, or do other creative projects. The Child Life staff and volunteers plan special craft activities throughout the month. You can also do art therapy with a real art therapist! And you're welcome to bring your own colouring books, crayons, or craft supplies from home too.
Who is everyone on my care team?

Your care team is like a dream team of helpers! Here are some of the people you might meet: your doctor (they're in charge of the big plan), your nurses (they take care of you day and night), a pharmacist (the medicine expert), a dietitian (the food expert), a physiotherapist (helps your body move), an occupational therapist (helps with everyday activities), a speech therapist (helps with talking and swallowing), a social worker (helps your family), a Child Life Specialist (helps you cope and play), an art therapist, a music therapist, and a Spiritual Care Practitioner. Not everyone will work with you, but the ones you need will be there!
Why do the nurses come check on me at night?

Even when you're fast asleep, a nurse will come by to check on you during the night. They do this to make sure you're comfortable, safe, and that everything is going well. They'll be as quiet as they can so they don't wake you up. It's just their way of taking care of you, even while you're dreaming!
Who is the person who made sure I could reach stuff from my bed and didn't fall?

That was probably your nurse! Nurses do a special check called a falls assessment to figure out if you might be at risk of falling. They make sure your bed rails are up, that you have slip-proof socks or slippers, and that everything you need is within easy reach. They also remind you to ask for help before getting up on your own. It's all about keeping you safe while you're here!
What does a pharmacist do at the hospital?

A pharmacist is the medicine expert! They make sure that all the medicines you get are the right ones, in the right amount. The Children's Hospital has its own pharmacy right on the first floor near the B1 entrance. If you or your parents ever have questions about a medicine, the pharmacist can explain everything. Your nurse can help arrange a visit with one.
I can't stop crying. I'm sorry.

Hey, you never ever have to say sorry for crying. Crying is your body's way of letting big feelings out, and that's actually a really healthy thing to do. Grown-ups cry in hospitals too — even really tough ones. Nobody here is going to think less of you for it. If you want, you can tell me or your nurse what's making you sad, or you can just let the tears come. Sometimes a good cry actually helps you feel a little bit better afterwards. You're being so brave just by being here.
Can my friend come visit me?

Friends can visit you at the hospital! Visiting depends on what unit you're on and how you're feeling, so it's a good idea for your parent to check with the nurses about the best time. And remember — your friend shouldn't come if they're feeling sick, because we need to keep everyone in the hospital healthy.
When do I get to eat?

At Children's Hospital, meals come at these times: breakfast is between 7:45 and 8:45 in the morning, lunch is between 11:45 and 12:45, and dinner is between 4:45 and 5:45. But here's something important — sometimes your doctor might need you to wait before eating, especially before certain tests. So always check with your nurse before munching on anything, okay?
What is the Heroes' Circle?

The Heroes' Circle is a super cool program at Children's Hospital! It runs all year long and visits kids in the hospital every week. You get to learn breathing exercises, relaxation techniques, and even some martial arts moves! It's designed to help you feel strong, calm, and powerful. Your brothers and sisters can try it too if they're visiting. It's a fun way to learn new skills that help you feel like a hero — even while you're in the hospital!
What are the food options for my parents?

Your parents can get food at a Tim Hortons spot called 'On the Go' on the second floor of Zone B — it's open on weekdays from 6:30 in the morning until 8 at night, but it's closed on weekends and holidays. There are also vending machines near the elevators on the first and third floors of Zone B. And if your family brings their own food, they can store it in the family fridge in the pantry rooms. Just remember to label everything with your name and the date!
Someone brought a machine to my bed and put stickers on my chest. Who was that?

That was probably a nurse or a technician. The stickers they put on your chest are called electrodes, and they connect to a machine that listens to how your heart is beating. It doesn't hurt at all — the stickers just sit on your skin. The person running the machine is specially trained to make sure everything looks good. If you have questions about what they're doing, it's always okay to ask them to explain!
Can my grandpa use a wheelchair here?

Yes! There are wheelchairs available near the hospital entrances. If your grandpa can't find one, he can ask a staff member or volunteer and they'll help him out. There are also drop-off points at the main doors so someone can let him out close to the entrance and then park the car.
There was a person in the family lounge who set up a coffee hour. Who was that?

That was probably a Child Life Specialist, a social worker, or a volunteer! The Culliton Family Lounge on B6-110 is a space for families on the B6 inpatient unit to relax and hang out. Special events like family coffee hours happen there so parents and caregivers can meet each other, take a break, and feel a little less alone. It's a nice way for families going through similar things to connect. If your parent wants to go to the next one, your nurse can tell them when it is!
What does it mean when they say Zone B?

The hospital is divided into different sections called zones, and each one has a letter. Children's Hospital is in Zone B! When you see a room number like B6-065, the B tells you it's in Zone B, the 6 tells you it's on the sixth floor, and 065 is the room number. Other parts of the bigger Victoria Hospital are in zones like C, D, and E. Knowing your zone and floor is like having a treasure map code that helps you find your way around!
Can a therapy dog come see me?

Children's Hospital works with St. John Ambulance to have therapy dogs visit certain units! These are specially trained dogs that come to help kids feel better. Ask your nurse or someone on your care team if a therapy dog visit is coming up — it's a really special treat.
Someone from the hospital showed up with toys when I was getting my needle. Why?

That was probably a Child Life Specialist or a nurse using a trick called distraction! It's part of Children's Hospital's Comfort Promise. When you're focused on something fun — like a toy, a video, or a game — your brain pays less attention to the needle. It's a real, proven way to make needle pokes feel less scary and less ouchy. Pretty clever, right? You can always ask for a distraction activity next time you need a needle.
What's a resident? Someone said they were a resident.

A resident is a person who has already finished medical school — so they're a real doctor — but they're still learning and practising to become even better at one special kind of medicine. At Children's Hospital, residents work with the main doctor (called the attending physician) and help take care of you. They're like doctors in training who are getting really good at helping kids. Your main doctor is always keeping an eye on everything they do!
The hospital smells weird. I don't like it.

You're right — hospitals do have a pretty unique smell! That smell usually comes from the special cleaning products they use to keep everything super clean and germ-free. It might seem strong, but it's actually a sign that people are working hard to keep you safe and healthy. Your nose will probably get used to it after a little while. And if you want, you can ask your parent to bring something that smells like home — like your favourite blanket or pillow!
Where can my mom get food?

There's a place called On the Go featuring Tim Hortons on the second floor of Zone B, in the main atrium. It's open on weekdays from 6:30 a.m. to 8:00 p.m., but it's closed on weekends and holidays. There are also vending machines near the elevators in Zone B on the 1st and 3rd floors.
Who answers the phone when my grandma calls the hospital?

When your grandma calls Children's Hospital, she'll first talk to the hospital operator — that's the person who answers the main phone number. The operator can connect her to the right place, like the floor you're staying on. Once the call gets to your unit, the unit clerk or your nurse can help. Your grandma will need to give your full name, and then she can ask to speak with your nurse. Sometimes it's hard to get through during shift changes — around 7 in the morning and 7 at night — so those aren't the best times to call!
I want to talk to someone but I don't know who.

I'm really glad you want to talk to someone — that takes courage. There are lots of people here who would love to listen. You could talk to your parent or whoever is with you, or tell your nurse how you're feeling. There are also Child Life Specialists at Children's Hospital who are specially trained to help kids work through big feelings, and they're really kind. If you want, you could even express yourself through art or music therapy. You don't have to figure everything out on your own. Just saying 'I need to talk' to any grown-up here is a perfect first step.
What does comfort positioning mean?

Comfort positioning is a way of sitting or being held during something like a needle poke that makes you feel safe and secure. Instead of lying flat and being held down, you get to sit up — maybe on your mom or dad's lap — in a big, warm hugging position. This helps you feel in control and less scared. The nurses at Children's Hospital believe this is much better than holding kids down, and research says so too! You and your family can talk to your nurse about the best comfort position for you.
What is that beeping sound I keep hearing?

Those beeping sounds come from machines called monitors. They keep track of things like how fast your heart is beating or how much oxygen is in your blood. The beeps are like little check-ins — the machine is saying 'everything's okay!' Sometimes a beep means a nurse should come take a look, but most of the time it's totally normal. If a beep ever worries you, you can always ask your nurse about it.
Why do different people ask me the same questions over and over?

It can feel annoying, right? But there's a really good reason! Each person on your care team needs to hear important things directly from you to make sure they have the right information. When they ask your name and birthday, it's to keep you safe. When different helpers ask how you're feeling, it's because they each take care of a different part of your health. Think of it like this: your nurse, your doctor, and your physiotherapist all need the information for different reasons — kind of like how your teachers at school each need to know different things about you!
The doctor scares me.

It's okay to feel that way. Doctors can seem a little serious or unfamiliar sometimes. But your doctor is on your team — their whole job is to help you feel better. Sometimes getting to know them a little helps. You could ask them a question, like what their favourite colour is or if they have any pets. Most doctors at Children's Hospital love talking to kids. And if you're really nervous, your parent or your nurse can always be right there with you when the doctor visits. You can even ask your parent to talk for you if you want.
What does a hospital room look like?

Your hospital room will have a special bed that can go up and down — which is pretty cool! There are buttons to move it. There will be a little table for your things, and rails on the side of the bed to keep you safe. You'll see a screen or monitor on the wall, and there might be some medical equipment nearby. There's also a spot where your mom, dad, or caregiver can sit or even sleep next to you. You can bring some of your favourite toys and books from home to make it feel more like your own space!
What is that clear liquid in the IV bag?

Most of the time, that clear liquid is a special fluid that helps keep your body hydrated — kind of like drinking water, but it goes straight to where your body needs it most. Sometimes medicine is mixed in too. Your nurse can tell you exactly what's in your bag if you're curious! It drips in slowly so your body can handle it well.
Who is the lady who talked to me and my siblings together?

That might have been a Child Life Specialist or a social worker. Both of these helpers work with your whole family — not just you. They know that when one kid is in the hospital, it can be tough for brothers and sisters too. They might have been talking to everyone about what's happening, answering questions, or just making sure your siblings feel included and okay. If any of you have more questions, you can always ask to talk to them again.
Someone came in and helped me play a game while the doctor was doing something. Why?

That person was using something called distraction — and it's part of the Comfort Promise at Children's Hospital! When you're focused on a fun game or activity, your brain doesn't pay as much attention to what the doctor is doing, which makes it feel less scary and less painful. The person helping you might have been a Child Life Specialist or a nurse. It's a trick that really works, and it's one of the ways the hospital keeps its promise to help you feel as comfortable as possible.
Someone came and talked to me about breathing and relaxation. Who was that?

That sounds like someone from the Heroes' Circle program! The Heroes' Circle visits kids at Children's Hospital every week and teaches really cool things like breathing exercises, relaxation tricks, and even some martial arts moves. These things can help you feel calmer and braver, especially when hospital stuff feels scary. If you liked it, you can ask your nurse about joining in next time they visit!
Can I eat snacks from home?

You might be able to, but you need to check with your care team first. Sometimes the doctors need you on a special diet, or there might be medical reasons you can't eat certain things. If your food is approved, your family can store it in the family fridge — just make sure to put your name and the date on it!
Who is the person who gave me medicine?

That was most likely your nurse. Nurses at Children's Hospital are the ones who give you your medicine and check on you throughout the day and night. Before they give you anything, they'll check your armband to make sure it's the right medicine for you. There are also pharmacists who work behind the scenes — they're the experts who prepare and check your medicine to make sure it's just right. If you ever have questions about your medicine, your nurse can get a pharmacist to come talk to you!
Why do I have to wear this bracelet?

That bracelet on your wrist is called an armband, and it's actually really important! It has your name, your birthday, and a special barcode on it. Before anyone gives you medicine or does a test, they scan or check your bracelet to make 100% sure they have the right person. It's like your own special hospital ID. If you have any allergies, you might get a red bracelet too, so everyone on your care team knows.
What happens during a physical check-up at the hospital?

During a check-up, the nurse or doctor will do a few things to see how your body is doing. They'll check your temperature with a thermometer, listen to your heart and lungs with a stethoscope, check your blood pressure with the arm squeezer, and look at how much oxygen is in your blood with the finger clip. They might also look in your ears, eyes, and mouth. None of these things hurt! They're just gathering information to make sure everything is working the way it should.
Everything is too much. I can't handle this.

It's okay to feel overwhelmed — there's a lot going on, and you're dealing with more than most kids your age have to deal with. You don't have to handle all of it at once. Let's take it one small step at a time. Right now, just take a few deep breaths with me. Breathe in slowly... and breathe out slowly. Good. You don't have to be strong every second. It's okay to ask for help. Tell your parent or your nurse that you're feeling overwhelmed, and they can help make things feel more manageable. You don't have to do this alone.
I met someone who said they help with 'transitions.' What does that mean?

That person is part of the Transitions in Care team! They help kids and families through big changes — like going from being a kid patient to an adult patient when you get older, or going from the hospital back to school. Transitions can feel confusing, so having someone who guides you through it makes everything smoother. Think of them as a bridge between where you are now and where you're going next!
Why is there a sink in every room?

Having a sink in every room makes it super easy for everyone to wash their hands. Remember, hand washing is the number one way to stop germs from spreading in a hospital! Nurses wash their hands before and after they help you, visitors should wash when they come in and leave, and you should wash yours too, especially before eating. That little sink does a really big job!
Can I bring my pet to visit?

Pets from home usually aren't allowed to visit the hospital, because it's important to keep all the patients, visitors, and staff safe and healthy. But in very special cases, a pet visit might be allowed with permission from the unit manager. There are also therapy dogs that visit sometimes — ask your care team if there's a therapy dog visit coming up!
Why does the doctor have other people following them around?

Great question! Those people might be medical students or residents. Medical students are grown-ups who are still in school learning how to become doctors. Residents have already finished medical school and are now practising to get even better at a special kind of medicine. They all work together as a team to take care of you, and the main doctor — called the attending physician — is in charge and makes sure everyone is doing a great job.
My mom went to get food. What if she doesn't come back?

Your mom is definitely coming back — she just needs to eat so she can have energy to be with you! It's like how you need to eat to feel strong. She probably went to grab something from Tim Hortons on the second floor or the vending machines, and she'll be back before you know it. While you wait, your nurses are right here taking care of you. If you start to feel really worried, you can press your call button and a nurse can come chat with you or even help you call your mom on the phone.
Why do doctors wear those pajama-looking clothes?

Those comfy-looking clothes are called scrubs! Doctors and nurses wear them because they're easy to move around in and super easy to wash. Since hospitals need everything to be really clean, scrubs can be washed at very high temperatures to get rid of all the germs. Plus, they don't have buttons or zippers that could get in the way when doctors are working. Pretty smart, right?
Can I bring my tablet?

You can bring your tablet! The hospital even has a patient entertainment site where you can watch live Rogers TV for free, or log in to your own streaming services if you have an account. You can also use the hospital's WiFi to stay connected.
Where can I find snacks on the floor?

If you're staying on the B6 inpatient unit, there are pantries in rooms B6-149 and B6-231 that have drinks and light snacks for patients. If you're at the Paediatric Medical Day Unit, they also provide light snacks for kids during day treatment. Just ask your nurse what's available!
When do I get breakfast?

Breakfast at Children's Hospital comes between 7:45 a.m. and 8:45 a.m. A grown-up on your care team will make sure you get a yummy meal! Sometimes the doctors need you to wait before eating, so your nurse will let you know if that's the case.
My friends are all playing soccer without me right now.

It's hard to know that life is going on out there while you're stuck in here. That feeling of missing out is real, and it's okay to be sad about it. But your friends aren't forgetting about you — they're probably talking about you and hoping you feel better soon. Soccer will be there when you're ready to play again. Right now, your body needs some time to heal. Maybe when you're feeling up to it, you could send your team a video message or have them sign a card for you.
Who takes care of really tiny babies in the hospital?

Really tiny babies are taken care of by a special team in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit — the NICU! The NICU has nurses, doctors, and other helpers who are experts at caring for the tiniest patients. They know exactly how to keep small babies warm, fed, and growing. Parents can be close to their baby too — there are special chairs for skin-to-skin cuddles, called kangaroo care, and sleeper chairs for resting right beside the baby.
Can my friend come visit me?

Friends can visit! But there are a few things to know. The hospital asks visitors to check with the nurses on your unit first to find out the best times for visiting. For inpatients, up to two care partners can be at your bedside at one time. Your friend should wash their hands when they come in and when they leave, and they shouldn't visit if they're feeling sick. But if everyone's healthy, visitors are welcome!
Can my mom or dad sleep here with me?

Yes! Most patient rooms at Children's Hospital have a spot where a parent or caregiver can sleep right near you. There are usually sleeper chairs or fold-out beds. Your parent will need their own pillow and can get clean sheets and blankets from the nurses. You won't have to be alone at night if you don't want to be. Just remember — you need to sleep in your own hospital bed so the nurses can check on you easily.
What should I NOT bring to the hospital?

There are a few things to leave at home: latex balloons, baby walkers, small toys that could be swallowed, electrical equipment you bring from home, and anything with perfume or a strong smell. This keeps you and all the other kids safe!
Who's the person who helped me get dressed and do things with my hands?

That's an occupational therapist — OT for short! Occupational therapists help kids do everyday things like getting dressed, using their hands, and being more independent. They might give you fun activities or exercises that help your fingers, hands, and arms work better. They're like a coach who helps you get better at the things you do every single day!
Someone talked to my parents about Indigenous healing. Who was that?

That was probably the Youth Indigenous Wellness Consultant! This person supports the mental health and cultural wellness of Indigenous kids at Children's Hospital. They help blend traditional ways of knowing with the care you get at the hospital. There's also a special Indigenous Healing Space in the hospital that's open to First Nations, Inuit, Métis, and Urban Indigenous families. If your family is interested, your care team can help you connect with them and visit the healing space.
I met someone who talked about a garden with butterflies. Who showed me that?

Someone on your care team or a volunteer probably told you about Alex's Butterfly Garden! It's a beautiful outdoor garden in Zone D on the second floor. It was created in honour of babies and infants, and it has benches and a soothing water fountain. It's a peaceful place where families, kids, and staff can go to sit quietly and enjoy nature. If you'd like to visit, ask your nurse or use the MazeMap app to find it!
Why did someone come to my room with a computer on wheels?

That computer on wheels is called a WOW — a Workstation on Wheels! Nurses and other members of your care team use it to look up your information, enter notes about how you're doing, and check which medicines you need. It helps them keep all your important details right at their fingertips. It's kind of like how teachers have a laptop to keep track of everything — except this one rolls right to your bed!
What is the SMILE Room?

The SMILE Room is one of the coolest rooms in the hospital! It's on the sixth floor in room B6-261, and it's full of awesome sensory stuff — like bubble columns that change colour, fibre optic lights you can hold, mirrors, and relaxing music. It's designed to help you relax or have fun with different sounds, lights, and textures. You can ask your nurse or a Child Life Specialist if you can visit it!
Where do I check in for my appointment?

When you get to the hospital, you go to Patient Registration on the second floor of Zone B. That's right above the main entrance. If you're not sure how to find it, look for the guide volunteers near the B1 entrance or B2 lobby — they're there on weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. to help!
Why did someone ask my mom if she wanted to talk to a lawyer?

That might have been a social worker telling your mom about a special program called Pro Bono Law Ontario. Children's Hospital has a partnership where families who need help with legal stuff — like paperwork, housing, or other problems that can affect your family — can talk to a lawyer for free. It doesn't mean anything is wrong! It's just another way the hospital tries to help families with things that might be stressful. Your mom can decide if she wants to use that help or not.
Can I use my tablet in the hospital?

Yes! You can bring your own tablet, phone, or device to use during your stay. The hospital even has a patient entertainment site where you can watch live TV for free or log in to your own streaming apps. If you need help with the WiFi, your parent or caregiver can call the Data Valet at 1-800-642-3958. Having your own stuff can make the hospital feel a lot more like home!
Where is the pharmacy?

The Children's Hospital Pharmacy is on the first floor near the B1 Entrance — the room is B1-001. It's open Monday to Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. (it's closed on holidays). If your doctor gives you a prescription, your family can fill it here before you leave!
Can I go outside while I'm in the hospital?

That depends on what your doctor says. Some kids can go to special areas like Alex's Butterfly Garden, which is a beautiful, peaceful outdoor garden in the hospital's D Zone on level 2. It has benches and a water fountain. But you'll need to check with your nurse first to make sure it's okay. If you can't go outside, there are still lots of fun indoor spaces to explore!
What is a family pantry?

The family pantry is a small room on the ward where your family can find drinks and light snacks. On the sixth floor, the pantries are in rooms B6-149 and B6-231. There's also a family fridge with a freezer where your family can store their own food — just make sure everything is labeled with your name and the date. It's a handy spot so your family doesn't always have to leave the floor to grab something to eat or drink!
I'm MAD. This isn't fair!

You're right to say how you feel — being in the hospital when you'd rather be doing other things is really frustrating. It's okay to be mad about it. Being angry doesn't make you a bad kid. It just means you're having big feelings about a tough situation. Sometimes it helps to squeeze a pillow, take some deep breaths, or draw a picture of how you're feeling. You can also talk to your parent, your nurse, or a Child Life Specialist about what's bugging you. They get it, and they want to help.
What if my parent doesn't speak English?

The hospital offers free interpreter services so your parent can talk to the doctors and nurses in the language they're most comfortable with. Your care team can arrange for an interpreter. Everyone deserves to understand what's happening, and the hospital wants to make sure your family does.
I need stitches and I'm scared.

It's really normal to be scared about stitches. But the good news is that your doctor will use special medicine to numb the area first, so you shouldn't feel the stitches going in. It might feel like a little pinch when they numb it, but after that, most kids say it just feels like a tugging sensation. You can hold your parent's hand, look away, or watch something fun on a screen while it happens. Your nurse can help you figure out the best way to stay comfortable. You've got this!
Who is the person who keeps checking my arm with the bracelet on it?

That's your nurse! Nurses are really important helpers here at Children's Hospital. They check your bracelet — called an armband — to make sure you're getting exactly the right care and medicine meant just for you. It has your name, your birthday, and a special barcode on it. Your nurse will check it before giving you medicine, doing a test, or taking you somewhere in the hospital. Think of it like a library card, but instead of checking out books, it helps the hospital keep track of how to help YOU.
My mom talked to someone about going back to school. Who was that?

That was probably someone from the Transitions in Care team or a social worker. They help figure out how to make going back to school easier after a hospital stay. They might talk to your mom about what to tell your teacher, how to handle homework you've missed, or whether the school needs to know about any health stuff. It's their job to help make sure school feels smooth and normal again when you're ready to go back!
What is a CT scan?

A CT scan is a special kind of picture that shows the inside of your body in really detailed slices — like slicing a loaf of bread and looking at each piece! You'll lie on a flat table that slides slowly into a big, donut-shaped machine. The machine spins around you, but you won't feel it. You just need to lie very still for a few minutes. It doesn't hurt at all! The pictures help the doctors see what's going on inside so they can take the best care of you.
What does the MazeMap app do?

MazeMap is a really cool map app that works like GPS but for inside the hospital! Your family can download it on a phone and search for the Victoria Hospital map. It shows you where everything is — rooms, elevators, washrooms, cafeterias, and more. You can also find maps on special screens called wayfinding kiosks around the hospital, or scan QR codes on posters near the elevators. It's super helpful for finding your way around this big place!
I don't want to fall asleep for the operation. What if I don't wake up?

That's a worry some kids have, and it's okay to talk about it. The special sleep you get during an operation is very different from regular sleep — it's carefully watched over by a whole team of doctors whose only job is to make sure you're safe the entire time. They use special tools to check on you every single second. Kids wake up from this kind of sleep every single day at this hospital. Your nurse, your doctor, or a Child Life Specialist can explain more about how it works if that would help you feel better. And remember, your family will be waiting for you when you wake up.
Why do some kids get to wear their own clothes?

Wearing your own comfy clothes from home can make you feel more like yourself! The hospital encourages kids to wear their own PJs, slippers, and clothes when it's possible. Sometimes you might need a hospital gown instead, like if you're going for a test or if there are tubes that need easy access. But most of the time, your own clothes are totally fine — bring your favourites!
What does it feel like to get blood taken?

Getting blood taken means a nurse or technician will use a small needle to take a little bit of blood from your arm, usually near your elbow. But remember the Comfort Promise! They'll put numbing cream on your skin first, so you feel a lot less. You can watch a video or look at something fun while it happens. You might feel a tiny pinch or some pressure, but it's over really quickly. Afterwards, they'll put a little bandage on the spot. You did it!
Who is the person who comes to play music?

That's a music therapist! They're a real trained musician who uses music to help kids in the hospital feel better. Music therapy can help with all sorts of things, like helping you relax or just having fun. You don't need to know how to play any instrument or sing — everyone can join in. It's one of the really special things about being at Children's Hospital.
What if I can't eat before a test?

Sometimes before certain tests or procedures, the doctors need your tummy to be empty, so they'll ask you not to eat or drink for a little while. This is called fasting, and your nurse will tell you and your family exactly when to stop eating and when you can eat again. It can be hard to wait, especially if you're hungry, but it's really important for keeping you safe during the test. As soon as it's okay, your nurse will let you know you can eat again!
Why do I have to wear this bracelet? It's uncomfortable.

That bracelet is actually really important — it's like your hospital ID card. It has your name, your birthday, and a special barcode on it. Every time a nurse gives you medicine or takes you for a test, they check your bracelet to make sure they have the right kid. It's one of the ways they keep you safe! I know it might feel a little annoying on your wrist, but it's doing an important job. If it's rubbing or feeling too tight, let your nurse know and they can adjust it for you.
Is there a quiet place I can go?

Yes! There's a place called the Sanctuary on the 3rd floor of Zone C (room C3-402). It's a calm, peaceful space where anyone can go for quiet time. It's open all day and all night, every day. There are also quiet rooms on the sixth floor (B6-119 and B6-257) — just ask your nurse before using them.
Can I bring too many toys?

It's best to bring just a few favourites rather than a whole bunch. Too many things in your room can create clutter, and that makes it harder for the nurses and doctors to take care of you. If you have too much stuff, some of it might need to go home with a visitor. A couple of special things is just right!
Can I bring my baby walker?

Baby walkers aren't allowed at the hospital. This is to keep everyone safe. If you need help walking or moving around, the hospital team has special equipment that's designed just for that. Your nurse can tell you more!
Will I have to wear a hospital gown?

Sometimes kids wear a hospital gown, which is a special loose shirt that the hospital gives you. It ties in the back and is really comfy and easy for the doctors and nurses to work with. But guess what — you can also wear your own pyjamas or comfy clothes from home a lot of the time! Your nurse will let you know if you need to put on a gown for something special, like a test or procedure. And don't forget to bring your own slippers or shoes too!
Can I play music at the hospital?

Children's Hospital actually has real music therapy! An accredited music therapist visits patients and uses music activities to help kids feel better. You don't need to know how to play any instruments — anyone can join in! Music therapy can help with things like feeling less pain, relaxing, and just having a good time. If you're interested, ask your nurse or a Child Life Specialist if the music therapist can visit you. You can also listen to your own music on your phone or tablet with headphones.
What floor am I on?

You can figure that out from your room number! The second number in your room tells you the floor. For example, if your room is B6-something, you're on the 6th floor of Zone B. If it's B2-something, you're on the 2nd floor. Pretty simple once you know the trick! And if you ever get turned around, any staff member can help you find your way.
Why do hospitals smell funny?

You know how your family might clean the kitchen with special cleaning sprays? The hospital uses special cleaners too — really strong ones — to make sure everything is super clean and free of germs. That's the smell you notice! It might seem funny, but it actually means the hospital is doing a good job keeping everything safe and clean for you.
Is there a place to play at the hospital?

Yes! There are fun places to play. If you're a younger kid, there's a cool nature-themed playroom called Ashley's Backyard on the sixth floor. If you're a bit older, there's the School-Age Activity Room where you can do crafts, play board games, build with LEGO, and do puzzles. There's even a special room called the SMILE Room that has bubble columns, fibre optics, mirrors, and music — it's like a magical sensory room! Your nurse can help you find these spaces.
What if I have to stay overnight?

Staying overnight at the hospital is called being an inpatient. You'll have your own bed in a room, and your mom, dad, or caregiver can stay right there with you — there's a sleeping spot for them in most rooms. You'll get meals brought to you, and the nurses will check on you during the night. You can wear your own pyjamas, have your favourite teddy with you, and even watch shows before bed. It might feel different from home, but the staff will do their best to make you comfortable.
What does the operating room look like?

The operating room is a very clean, bright room with special lights above a bed in the middle. You'll see people wearing masks, caps on their heads, and special clothes. There are machines and screens around the room that help the doctors during the operation. It might look a little different from regular rooms, but everyone in there is there to help you. The team will talk to you, help you feel comfortable, and make sure you know what's happening.
Why can't I bring perfume or smelly things?

Children's Hospital is a fragrance-free place. That means nobody is supposed to wear perfume, body spray, or use other strong-smelling products. This is because some patients and staff are really sensitive to smells — it can give them headaches, make it hard to breathe, or make them feel sick. So when you come to the hospital, just use unscented soap and shampoo. It helps keep the air comfortable and safe for everyone!
What happens if I have an allergy?

If you have allergies, the hospital will make sure everyone knows about them. You'll get a special red bracelet to wear — it's different from your regular armband. This red allergy bracelet tells every single person on your care team about your allergies so they can keep you safe. Your nurses and doctors will ask you about allergies when you arrive, and they'll make sure your food and medicines are all safe for you. Always tell someone if you have allergies, even if you think they already know!
They're putting medicine in my IV. Will it hurt?

Most kids don't feel anything when medicine goes in through the IV — it's like invisible help flowing into your body. You might feel a cool sensation in your arm, and very occasionally some medicines can make you feel a little funny for a moment. If anything hurts or feels weird, tell your nurse right away — that's really important. But most of the time, the medicine goes in and you don't feel it at all. The IV does all the work so you don't have to get another poke. Pretty smart, right?
Why do people keep telling me to use hand gel?

The hand gel (hand sanitizer) is the hospital's best tool for fighting germs. Hospitals have to be extra careful about germs because sick kids can catch things more easily. Using hand gel before going into a room and when leaving is one of the most important things everyone can do — including you! It only takes a few seconds.
Can my grandma bring homemade cookies?

That's sweet of your grandma! But before you eat anything that's brought from home, you need to check with your care team first. Sometimes kids in the hospital have to be on a special diet or can't eat certain things for medical reasons. If the team says it's okay, you can enjoy them! Just make sure to put any leftovers in the family fridge with your name and the date on them.
They said I need another operation. I already did one!

That must feel really frustrating — you already went through it once and now you have to do it again. It's totally okay to feel upset about that. But here's something that might help: you already know you CAN do it, because you did it before! You're already an expert. And your care team knows you better now too, so they can help make this time even smoother. Talk to your nurse or a Child Life Specialist about how you're feeling, and they can help you prepare. You're tougher than you think.
The nurse used big words I don't understand.

Hospital words can sound pretty confusing — even grown-ups sometimes don't know what they mean! It's always, always okay to ask someone to explain things in a way that makes more sense to you. You could say something like, 'Can you tell me that in kid words?' Nurses and doctors are happy to explain things differently. You could also ask your parent to help translate the big words. Understanding what's happening is important, and you should never feel embarrassed about asking.
Can my teacher visit me?

Your teacher can visit as long as they follow the visitor rules — they should check with the nurses about the best time, wash their hands when they come in and when they leave, and make sure they aren't feeling sick. It's really nice when familiar people come to see you!
Someone said they were a 'nurse practitioner.' Is that the same as a nurse?

That's a really smart question! A nurse practitioner is similar to a nurse, but they've done extra schooling so they can do some of the things doctors do too. At Children's Hospital, nurse practitioners work closely with the doctors to plan your care. Think of them as being right in between a nurse and a doctor — they're like a super-powered nurse who can help figure out what's going on with your body and decide on the best plan to help you feel better.
What do I need to bring for my appointment?

For your appointment, your parent should bring your Ontario health card, your appointment card or letter, any medicine you're taking, your family doctor's name and phone number, and any medical papers like X-rays or referral letters. You can bring a favourite book or toy to keep you busy while you wait!
I feel lonely.

Feeling lonely in the hospital is something a lot of kids experience, and it's okay to say it out loud. Even though there are people around, it's not the same as being home with your friends and family. If you're feeling up to it, you might enjoy visiting one of the activity rooms where other kids hang out — there's one with games, LEGO, and crafts on the sixth floor. You can also ask about Upopolis, which is a safe website for kids in the hospital to chat with other kids across Canada. And your family and friends can call or visit you too.
Why does one nurse leave and a new one shows up?

Great observation! Nurses take turns caring for you in something called shifts. One nurse takes care of you during the day, and then a different nurse takes over at night. When they switch — which happens around 7 in the morning and 7 in the evening — the two nurses talk right at your bedside to share everything about how you're doing. This is called a shift change report, and your mom, dad, or caregiver can listen in and ask questions too. That way, your new nurse knows everything about you!
What is a cast?

A cast is a hard shell that goes around a broken bone to keep it still and safe while it heals. A doctor or technician will wrap your arm or leg with special materials that start soft and wet but then dry and get really hard. You might get to choose a colour! Once it's on, your bone can rest and grow back together inside. The cast might feel heavy and itchy sometimes, but you need to keep it on until the doctor says your bone is all better. Some kids get their friends to sign their cast!
Can I bring my stuffed animal to the hospital?

Absolutely! Bringing a favourite stuffed animal or comfort toy from home is a great idea. It can make your hospital room feel more cozy. Just make sure it's clean — the hospital likes toys that can be wiped down or washed easily. Try not to bring too many things though, because there isn't a huge amount of space. Your special stuffie should stay with you and not be shared with other kids, to keep everyone healthy.
What if I'm still here for Christmas?

I can see why that would be on your mind. Missing Christmas at home would be really hard. But even if you are here, Children's Hospital tries to make holidays special for kids. There are special events, activities, and lots of people who want to make sure kids here still feel the holiday magic. And your family can visit and bring some of your favourite traditions to you. Your care team is also working hard to get you better and home as quickly as possible. It's always okay to talk to your nurse or parent about how you're feeling.
Why do I have to wash my hands so much?

Washing your hands is like having a superpower against germs! In a hospital, keeping hands clean is extra important because germs can spread easily and make people who are already not feeling well even sicker. You should wash your hands before eating, after using the bathroom, and whenever you enter or leave a room. The hospital has special hand sanitizer stations everywhere to make it easy.
How do I find my way around this place?

The hospital has lots of helpers for that! You can find information desks that are open Monday to Friday from 8 in the morning to 8 at night, and there are friendly guide volunteers near the B1 entrance and B2 lobby. There's also an app called MazeMap that has a map of the whole hospital — your parent can download it on their phone. And there are QR codes you can scan near the elevators to pull up a map too!
What happens when I leave the hospital?

When it's time to go home — which is called being discharged — your care team will talk to your family about everything you need to know. They'll explain any medicines you need to take, when to come back for a check-up, and what to watch for at home. Make sure your family brings your car seat, because you need one to ride in the car! Before you leave, double-check that you've packed up all your toys and things. And don't forget to say goodbye to your nurses if you want to!
Can my mom or dad sleep at the hospital with me?

Yes! Children's Hospital knows how important it is to have your family close by. Most rooms have a spot where your mom, dad, or caregiver can sleep right next to you. They'll get clean sheets, pillows, and blankets. But here's an important rule — you need to sleep in your own hospital bed, not with your grown-up, because the nurses need to be able to reach you easily. Your grown-up will be right beside you the whole night, though!
I'm having surgery and I'm really really scared.

It makes total sense to feel scared before surgery. Even grown-ups feel nervous about it. Here at Children's Hospital, they have a special program where your mom or dad might be able to come into the operating room with you while you fall asleep — you can ask your care team about that. Before the surgery, you'll meet the people who will be taking care of you, and they'll explain everything that's going to happen. They might also give you something to help you feel relaxed and sleepy. You won't feel anything during the surgery. Talk to your nurse about how you're feeling — they're really good at helping kids feel braver.
Is there an app to find my way around the hospital?

Yes! You can download the MazeMap app and search for the Victoria Hospital map. It helps you and your family find your way around. There are also wayfinding kiosks inside the hospital and QR codes on posters near the elevators that you can scan.
What is a wheelchair for?

A wheelchair helps people get around when they can't walk easily — maybe because they're tired, hurt their leg, or just had a procedure. The hospital has wheelchairs you can borrow, usually near the entrances. If you can't find one, just ask a staff member or volunteer and they'll help. Some kids even think it's fun to zoom around in one!
What sounds will I hear in the hospital?

The hospital has lots of interesting sounds! You might hear beeping from machines that help the doctors and nurses watch over patients. You might hear people talking, shoes squeaking on the shiny floors, and sometimes a ding from an elevator. There might also be announcements on a speaker, kind of like at school. If you're near the babies' area, you might hear little babies crying. All these sounds are normal! If any sound worries you, just ask your grown-up or a nurse what it is.
I'm really scared of getting a needle.

It's totally okay to feel scared about needles — lots of kids feel that way, even really brave ones. Here at Children's Hospital, your care team has something called the Comfort Promise. That means they'll do everything they can to make it hurt less. They can put a special numbing cream on your skin so you barely feel anything, and they can help you sit in a cozy position — maybe on your mom or dad's lap. You could also watch a funny video or squeeze a stress ball while it happens. You don't have to be tough about it. Just tell your nurse how you're feeling and they'll help you through it.
Can I bring my glasses to the hospital?

You should definitely bring your glasses! The hospital guide says to bring any important medical aids like eyeglasses, hearing aids, braces, or crutches. You need to be able to see clearly, so don't forget to pack them.
Do I need a car seat to go home?

Yes! It's the law that all children must travel in an approved car seat. Make sure your parent brings your car seat when they come to pick you up. The hospital even has a Car Seat Program with special helpers who can make sure your car seat is put in correctly.
I'm afraid of dogs. What if one comes to my room?

That's a really good thing to mention! The therapy dogs that visit Children's Hospital through St. John's Ambulance are very gentle and well-trained, but nobody will ever force you to be around one. If you're afraid of dogs, just let your nurse know, and they'll make sure a therapy dog doesn't come to your room. Everyone has their own likes and dislikes, and the hospital respects that. Some kids love the dogs and some don't, and both are perfectly okay.
What is the hand sanitizer for?

The hand sanitizer dispensers you see everywhere are filled with a special alcohol-based gel that kills germs on your hands in seconds. It's the fastest way to clean your hands in the hospital! You should use it before going into a patient room, when leaving a room, and before eating. Just squirt some on and rub your hands together — easy peasy!
What is Ashley's Backyard?

Ashley's Backyard is a special playroom on the sixth floor in room B6-259! It has a nature theme, so it feels like you're playing outside even though you're inside the hospital. It's designed for younger kids — babies, toddlers, and preschoolers — and their families to relax and play together. You can go there during the day and in the evening, but a grown-up needs to be with you. It's a nice break from your hospital room!
Who set up the TV and helped me watch shows in my room?

Your nurse or a staff member helped you get set up! Children's Hospital has a patient entertainment site where you can watch live Rogers TV for free. If your family has accounts for streaming services, you can use those too. If you have any trouble getting the TV or entertainment to work, you can ask your nurse or stop by an information desk for help. Having shows to watch can make the time go by a lot faster!
What is the Paediatric Family Resource Centre?

The Paediatric Family Resource Centre is a special room on the first floor of Zone B, in room B1-006. It's a quiet place where you and your family can find information about different health topics, use the internet, and get help and support from friendly people who understand what it's like to have a kid in the hospital. It's open most days of the week, and on Saturdays and Sundays by appointment. If you or your family need a calm place to take a break or look something up, it's a great spot to visit!
Who are the people in the colourful clothes?

Those colourful clothes are called scrubs! Lots of people at the hospital wear them — doctors, nurses, and other helpers. They're comfy and easy to keep clean. Different people might wear different colours, but everyone who takes care of you is part of your care team. If you're ever not sure who someone is, it's totally okay to ask them! They all wear name tags too, so you can see their name and what their job is.
Why does the nurse check on me at night?

Even when you're sleeping, your nurse peeks in to make sure you're comfortable and safe. They might quickly check your temperature or listen to how you're breathing. They try to be super quiet so they don't wake you up! It's actually a really nice thing — even in the middle of the night, someone is watching out for you.
It's too loud and too bright. I want it to stop.

Hospitals can be a lot for your senses — all the lights and sounds and people. It's okay to feel overwhelmed by it. Let's see what we can do. Your nurse might be able to dim the lights in your room, and you could ask for the door to be closed to block out hallway noise. If you have headphones, listening to music or a story can help too. There's also a room on the sixth floor called the SMILE Room that has calm lights and soothing music — you could ask if you can visit when you're feeling up to it. Tell your nurse how you're feeling so they can help.
What are the Bravery Beads?

Bravery Beads are a really cool program! Each bead represents something you've been through in the hospital — like a test, a treatment, or a brave moment. You collect them to make a special necklace or string that tells YOUR unique story. Kids of all ages can join the program if they want — it's totally voluntary.
Nobody from my class has called me.

That must feel really lonely, and I'm sorry. Sometimes your friends might not know that you want them to call, or their parents might not have your hospital number. Maybe your mom or dad could reach out to your teacher and let them know it would cheer you up to hear from your classmates. A lot of times, classes will make cards or send messages once they know you'd like that. Your friends haven't forgotten you — they might just not know the best way to reach you right now. You're definitely not forgotten.
Can my family bring me a birthday cake?

That's a nice idea! But before anyone brings food from outside, your care team needs to check if it's safe for you to eat. Some kids are on special diets or have allergies. Ask your nurse first, and if they say yes, you can celebrate! Just remember the hospital is fragrance-free, so no scented candles.
Why do nurses come check on me at night when I'm sleeping?

Your nurses check on you during the night because it's their job to make sure you're safe and comfortable — even while you're snoozing! They might look at a monitor, check your temperature, or just peek in to see that you're doing okay. It's kind of like how your mom or dad might check on you at night at home. Your nurse is always nearby, day and night, to help if you need anything.
I don't want a needle! Please no needles!

I hear you — needles can feel really scary, and it's okay to say that. You're not being silly at all. The nurses here know that needles are one of the hardest parts for kids, and they have special ways to help. They can use a cream that makes your skin feel sleepy so it doesn't hurt as much, and they'll let you pick something fun to look at or hold while it happens. You can also ask your mom, dad, or whoever is with you to hold your hand. Tell your nurse exactly how you feel — they really want to make it easier for you.
I saw someone with a pager clipped to their clothes. Who uses pagers?

Lots of people at Children's Hospital still use pagers! Doctors, Spiritual Care Specialists, and other team members carry them so they can be reached quickly anywhere in the hospital. A pager is like a tiny phone that just gets short messages. When someone needs a particular helper fast, they send a page, and that person knows to come right away. It's one of the ways the hospital makes sure help is never far away!
People keep telling me I'm brave but I don't feel brave.

You know what's funny about bravery? The people who are the bravest usually don't feel brave at all. Being brave isn't about not being scared — it's about getting through something hard even though you ARE scared. And that's exactly what you're doing every single day in the hospital. So even though you don't feel brave inside, from the outside, everyone can see just how strong you are. It's okay to not feel brave. You're still doing an incredible job, and it's okay if some days are harder than others.
Do I get to pick my food?

Yes! You'll get a form on your breakfast tray where you can choose what you'd like to eat the next day. It's like a little menu. The choices will be based on what your doctor says is okay for you to eat. If you have a food allergy or something you can't eat, let your nurse know and they'll make sure your meals are safe.
Who is the person who let me use a laptop?

That was probably a Child Life Specialist! At Children's Hospital, Child Life Services has laptops that patients can borrow. There's even a cool website called Upopolis — it's a safe social network just for kids ages 8 to 18 who are in hospitals across Canada. You can connect with other kids going through similar stuff. If you want to use a laptop again, just ask a Child Life Specialist!
Who are all the different nurses and why are there different types?

There are two main types of nurses you might meet: Registered Nurses (RNs) and Registered Practical Nurses (RPNs). Both of them take great care of you — they give medicine, check on you, and make sure you're doing okay. RNs have a bit more schooling and can do some extra things. Then there are Nurse Practitioners, who have done even MORE school and can do some things that doctors do, like figuring out what might be making you sick. They all work together like a team of superheroes, each with a different level of power!
There's a room called the SMILE Room. Who takes me there?

A Child Life Specialist or your nurse can help you get to the SMILE Room! It's a really cool room on the sixth floor in room B6-261. It's filled with amazing things like bubble columns, fibre optics, mirrors, and music. It's designed to help you relax or feel more alert, depending on what you need. It's called the SMILE Room because it's hard not to smile when you're in there! Ask your care team if you can visit.
Where does my family park the car?

Your family will most likely park in the parking garage called Parking Lot P8. It's right near Children's Hospital and you get to it from Baseline Road. When you drive in, a machine gives you a ticket. When it's time to leave, your grown-up pays for the ticket at a machine by the elevators on the second floor of the garage. There are also other parking lots around the hospital. And don't worry — if it's hard to walk from the car, there are drop-off spots right at the entrance where someone can let you out before parking.
Someone came and helped me do art. Is she a teacher?

She's kind of like a teacher, but her special job title is art therapist! The art therapy program at Children's Hospital lets kids like you draw, paint, and create things to help express how you're feeling. Sometimes it's easier to show your feelings through a picture than with words, right? Art therapy can help you feel more relaxed and in control, even when hospital stuff feels unpredictable. You can ask your nurse if the art therapist can visit again.
Who are the people wearing scrubs?

Lots of people at Children's Hospital wear scrubs — those are the comfy-looking pyjama-like outfits you see! Doctors, nurses, surgeons, and many other helpers wear them. Scrubs are worn because they're easy to keep clean, comfortable to work in all day, and they can be washed at very high temperatures to kill germs. So when you see someone in scrubs, it usually means they're someone who's here to help take care of patients like you!
This is taking forever. I'm never getting out of here.

I know it can feel that way when every day seems to go by so slowly. Waiting is one of the hardest parts of being in the hospital. But your doctors are keeping track of how you're doing, and they'll let you go home as soon as it's safe. In the meantime, try to find little things to look forward to each day — a favourite show, a visit from someone you love, or a fun activity. Ask your nurse if there's a plan for when you might go home. Having something to look forward to can make the waiting a little more bearable.
What if my mom has to leave? I don't want to be alone.

That's a really understandable worry. The good news is that your mom or another family member can stay with you a lot of the time — many rooms here at Children's Hospital even have a place for a parent to sleep overnight. And even if your mom does need to step out for a little while, you won't really be alone. Your nurses check on you regularly, even during the night, to make sure you're okay. If you ever feel lonely or need something, you can press the call button and a nurse will come to you.
What are the visiting rules if someone in the room next to me is sick?

Visiting rules are set up to protect everyone. If someone nearby needs extra germ protection, the nurses might have special instructions — like wearing a mask or gown. If you see a sign outside someone's room, don't go in without checking with a nurse first. And always, always wash your hands!
Why does the blood pressure cuff squeeze my arm?

That squeezy thing is a blood pressure cuff! It puffs up like a balloon around your arm to check how hard your heart is pumping blood through your body. It squeezes for just a little bit and then lets go. It might feel tight and funny, but it's totally safe and it's over really quick. Think of it as your arm getting a quick hug!
Why does my nurse check my bracelet before everything?

Your nurse checks your bracelet every single time before giving you medicine, doing a test, or taking you somewhere. It has your name, birthday, and a special barcode on it. They scan it or read it to make absolutely sure they're giving the right thing to the right kid. It's one of the most important safety rules!
Is there a place my family can hang out together?

Yes! The Culliton Family Lounge (B6-110) is a space where patients on the B6 inpatient unit can relax and spend time with family or friends. Sometimes they have special group events and family coffee hours there too. There's also the Paediatric Family Resource Centre on the 1st floor of Zone B.
Who is the person who brought me food on a tray?

That person works with Patient Food Services! Their job is to bring meals to kids who are staying in the hospital. The kitchen team makes your breakfast, lunch, and dinner, and they bring it right to you. Breakfast usually comes around quarter to 8 in the morning, lunch comes before 1 in the afternoon, and dinner comes around 5 in the evening. If you're on a special diet, the food team works with your doctor and nurse to make sure you get exactly the right food.
Can I bring my own pillow from home?

Yes, you can! Bringing your own pillow, blanket, or even a favourite pajama set can make your hospital bed feel a lot more like your bed at home. Just make sure it's clean and washable. The hospital provides pillows and blankets too, but sometimes your own stuff just feels better. Label it with your name so it doesn't get mixed up!
What is the butterfly garden?

Alex's Butterfly Garden is a really beautiful outdoor space in D Zone, Level 2 of the hospital. It has plants, benches, and a soothing water fountain. It was created for families to have a quiet, peaceful place to sit and think. It's named in honour of babies who were very sick, and it's a special place where families can feel calm. You can ask your nurse if you can visit it!
I keep waking up at night and I'm scared.

Waking up in an unfamiliar place at night can feel really unsettling. That's completely okay. Remember, your nurses are nearby all night long, and they actually check on you during the night to make sure you're doing well. If you wake up and feel scared, you can press the call button next to your bed and someone will come. If your parent is staying overnight, they'll be right there too. Sometimes it helps to have a small light on or hold onto a comfort item from home. You're safe here, even when it's dark.
What is numbing cream?

Numbing cream is a special cream or gel that the nurse puts on your skin before a needle poke. It makes that little spot on your skin feel kind of sleepy, so when the needle comes, you feel way less of it — or sometimes nothing at all! It's part of something called the Comfort Promise at Children's Hospital. The cream needs a little bit of time to work, so the nurse will put it on and then wait before doing the needle part.
Someone came in and cleaned the table and door handles in my room. Why?

That was someone from the housekeeping or environmental services team, and what they're doing is super important! They clean things like tables, door handles, and bed rails because those are spots where germs love to hang out. By wiping everything down regularly, they help stop germs from moving from one person to another. It's one of the biggest ways the hospital keeps you and all the other patients healthy. Those cleaners are real germ-fighting champions!
Who is the person who helped my mom stay with me overnight?

That was your nurse or another member of your care team! At Children's Hospital, they know how important it is for families to be together. Most patient rooms have a spot for a parent or caregiver to sleep — like a fold-out chair or a special sleep space with clean sheets, pillows, and blankets. Your nurse helps set that up and lets your parent know the rules, like staying in the room between 8 at night and 8 in the morning. Your parent can be right there beside you!
Who is the person who checked if my car seat was safe?

That was a Car Seat Technician! Children's Hospital has specially trained people who check car seats to make sure they're put in the right way. They can meet with your family in person or even do it over a video call. Making sure your car seat is installed properly is really important so you're super safe on the ride home. Your nurse can help your family set up a time to meet with a Car Seat Technician if you need one!
I like my nurse. What if I get a different one tomorrow?

It's so nice that you've connected with your nurse! Nurses work in shifts, so you might have different nurses at different times. But every nurse on the team knows about you and your care plan, and they'll all be kind and take good care of you. During shift change, your nurses share information about you so the next nurse knows exactly what you need. And there's a good chance you'll see your favourite nurse again on another shift. You could even make them a drawing to say thanks when they're back!
I don't want to eat. I feel sick.

That's okay — sometimes when your body isn't feeling well, eating is the last thing you want to do. You don't have to force it. But it's important to tell your nurse that you're feeling sick and don't want to eat, because they need to know. Your doctor and nurse can figure out the best way to help your tummy feel better. Sometimes starting with small sips of water or a tiny bit of crackers can help. Just be honest about how you're feeling, and your care team will take it from there.
I don't like it when new people come in my room.

I understand — it can feel a little overwhelming when lots of different people come to see you, especially people you don't know. At a teaching hospital like this one, there are doctors, nurses, students, and other team members who all work together to help you. Every person who comes in is there because they care about you getting better. It's always okay to ask someone who they are and what they're doing. And if you feel uncomfortable, tell your parent or nurse — they can help.
Can my daddy stay with me tonight?
