Lots of rooms at Children's Hospital have a place for a parent to sleep overnight — like a special chair or a small bed right next to yours. Your daddy can talk to your nurse about the sleeping arrangements on your unit. If he's able to stay, he'll be right there with you. And even if he has to go home for a little while, your nurses will be watching over you all night. You won't be alone. Just let your nurse know how you're feeling, okay?
Why do some rooms have signs on the door?

Some rooms have special signs when a patient needs extra germ protection. If you see a sign, it means there are extra rules — like wearing gloves, a gown, or a mask before going in. It's nothing scary, it's just to keep germs from spreading. If you see a sign on someone's room, stop at the nurses' station first and they'll tell you what to do.
When does the front door lock?

The main entrance to Children's Hospital (the B Tower entrance) is open from 6:00 in the morning until 8:30 at night. After that, you need to check in with the security guard to get inside. If your parent is coming through the parking garage, that entrance is open 24 hours, but they still need to check in with security after hours.
I just want to be a normal kid.

You ARE a normal kid — a normal kid who happens to be in the hospital right now. Being here doesn't change who you are. You still like the same things, you're still you, and when your body has healed up, you'll go right back to your normal life. Lots and lots of kids have hospital stays, and they go on to do all the normal kid things afterwards. This is just a chapter in your story, not the whole book. And while you're here, you can still do tons of normal kid things — play, laugh, watch shows, and hang out with people you love.
What does it feel like to ride in a hospital bed?

If you need to go somewhere in the hospital, sometimes the nurses will wheel your whole bed there! The bed has wheels on the bottom, and it feels a little like a slow ride. You might see the ceiling tiles going by above you and hear the wheels rolling on the floor. The nurses will guide the bed carefully through hallways and into elevators. It might feel different, but you'll be safe the whole time, and you can bring your stuffed animal along for the ride!
What does a pharmacist do at the hospital?

A pharmacist is a medicine expert! At Children's Hospital, the pharmacy is on the first floor near the B1 entrance. Pharmacists make sure your medicine is exactly right — the right kind, the right amount, and safe for you. They also help your family understand how to give you medicine when you go home. If your family has questions about any medicine, your nurse can ask a pharmacist to come and explain everything. They're like the medicine detectives of the hospital!
Can both my parents visit me?

You can have up to two care partners at your bedside at the same time when you're staying overnight. So both your parents can be with you! The nurses might ask them to step out for a little while if they need to do something for your care, but they can come right back.
Where can I make a phone call?

You can use your own phone, or the hospital has patient telephones you can use for free to make local and toll-free calls. If you need a private spot to make a call, the quiet rooms on the sixth floor (B6-119 and B6-257) can be used for that. Just check with your nurse first.
Why can't my friend come when they have a cold?

When someone is sick — even with just a cold — they can spread germs to the kids in the hospital who are already not feeling well. The hospital asks that anyone who is sick or has been feeling sick in the last week not visit. It's a really important rule to protect you and all the other kids here.
What if we don't have a car seat?

All kids have to ride in an approved car seat — it's the law! If you need help making sure your car seat is installed the right way, the hospital's Trauma Program has trained Car Seat Technicians who can check it for you. Your nurse can tell your family how to schedule a car seat check.
What are Bravery Beads?

Bravery Beads are really special! They're beads you collect to make a necklace or string that tells your personal hospital story. Each bead stands for something you went through — like getting an IV, having a test done, or being really brave during a procedure. Over time, you build up this amazing collection that shows everything you've been through. It's your very own bravery necklace!
What happens when I'm ready to leave the hospital?

When it's time to go home, your care team will tell you and your parents all about how to take care of you at home — like what medicines you need, what food to eat, and when to come back for a check-up. Make sure to bring a car seat if you need one, and pack up all your things! Your nurse will go over everything before you leave.
There's a person who helps kids who speak different languages. Who is that?

That's an interpreter! Children's Hospital has free interpretation services so that every family can communicate with their care team in a language they're comfortable with. The interpreter translates what the doctors and nurses say so your family can understand everything about your care. If your family speaks a language other than English, or if someone is deaf or hard of hearing, your care team can arrange for an interpreter anytime. Just ask!
What is an IV?

An IV stands for 'intravenous,' which is a big word that means 'into a vein.' It's a tiny, thin tube that goes into a small vein, usually in your hand or arm. Through that tube, doctors can give you medicine or fluids your body needs without you having to swallow anything. Getting the IV put in might pinch for a second, but after that it usually doesn't hurt. If it ever bothers you, tell your nurse right away!
Someone showed me the MazeMap app on a phone. Who was that?

That could have been anyone on your care team — a nurse, a volunteer, or an information desk helper! MazeMap is an app that has a map of the whole Victoria Hospital and Children's Hospital inside it. It helps families find their way around the big building. You can also use the wayfinding kiosks around the hospital or scan a QR code on posters near the elevators. It's like a treasure map for finding your way around the hospital!
Who is the person who helped me when I was really scared before my surgery?

That was probably a Child Life Specialist! Their job is to help you feel less scared about things like surgery. They might have explained what would happen, let you see or touch some of the equipment, or taught you breathing tricks to calm down. At Children's Hospital, there's also a program where a parent can come with you into the operating room while you fall asleep — that's called the Parental Presence at Anaesthesia Induction program. Your care team wants you to feel as brave and calm as possible!
I don't want a roommate. I want my own room.

Sharing a room with someone else can feel awkward, especially when you're not feeling great. The hospital tries to give people the room they want, but sometimes it depends on what's available. If sharing a room is really bothering you, your parent can talk to the nurse about it. In the meantime, your nurse can close the curtain around your bed to give you more privacy. And who knows — sometimes roommates turn out to be pretty cool. But your feelings are completely valid, and it's okay to want your own space.
Where does my parent sleep?

Most rooms have a special spot where your parent can sleep right next to you. They'll get clean sheets, pillows, and blankets. But the rule is that your parent sleeps in their own spot and you sleep in your hospital bed — that way the nurses can reach you easily if they need to.
What happens if I get lost in the hospital?

The hospital is really big, but there are lots of people who can help you if you feel lost! There are information desks with friendly helpers, and there are guide volunteers wearing special outfits near the main entrances. You can also look for any hospital staff member — they all wear name tags and will be happy to help. There are also maps on the walls and special screens called wayfinding kiosks. Just remember, your room number tells you your zone and floor, like B2 means Zone B, floor 2!
When is dinner served here?
Dinner time at the hospital is between 4:45 p.m. and 5:45 p.m. That might feel a little earlier than dinner at home, but it gives you plenty of time to enjoy your meal and relax for the evening.
What if I don't like the food?

If you don't enjoy what you get, let your nurse know! The hospital offers different kinds of diets and they really try to give you things you'll like. You get to pick your meals on a form that comes with your breakfast tray. If something doesn't taste good to you, it's totally okay to speak up.
What happens when I get to the emergency room?

When you arrive at the Emergency Department, you and your grown-up will walk through a special doorway. There's a gentle walk-through system that checks for safety — kind of like going through an airport, but you don't have to take off your shoes or empty your pockets! Then a nurse called a triage nurse will talk to you and your family to find out what's going on and how quickly you need help. You might have to wait a little while, and that's normal. Your grown-up will stay with you the whole time.
What are vital signs?

Vital signs are measurements that show how your body is doing. The main ones are your temperature (how warm you are), your heart rate (how fast your heart is beating), your blood pressure (how hard your blood is pushing through your body), your breathing rate (how fast you're breathing), and your oxygen level (how much oxygen is in your blood). The nurse checks these regularly using tools like the thermometer, blood pressure cuff, and the little finger clip. It only takes a couple of minutes and doesn't hurt!
What does it smell like when they clean my skin before a needle?

Before a needle, the nurse might wipe your skin with a little wet pad that smells like rubbing alcohol. It's a sharp, clean smell that goes away pretty quickly. The wipe might feel cool on your skin for a second. This cleaning step gets rid of any germs on your skin before the needle goes in. If they're using the Comfort Promise numbing cream, that goes on first and doesn't have much of a smell at all.
What is the elevator like?

The hospital has big elevators that can fit lots of people — even people in wheelchairs or hospital beds! When you step inside, you'll see buttons for each floor. The elevators might ding when the doors open, and you might feel a little funny in your tummy when it goes up or down — like in any elevator. Near the elevators, you'll find signs and even QR codes on posters that you can scan with a phone to see a map of the hospital.
Can I bring my favourite blanket?

Yes! Bringing your own blanket is a great idea to help you feel comfortable and cozy. The hospital gives you blankets too, but your special one from home can make things feel a little more normal. Just make sure it's clean when you bring it.
Why can't I bring my own balloons?

That's a really good question! Some balloons are made of a material called latex, and some people are very allergic to it. An allergic reaction can make someone really sick. So to keep every kid in the hospital safe, latex balloons aren't allowed. But don't worry — if someone wants to send you something fun, they can bring mylar balloons (the shiny, foil kind) or other cool gifts instead!
I don't feel like me.

Being in the hospital can make everything feel a little topsy-turvy, and it makes sense that you might not feel like your normal self right now. Your body is working really hard to get better, and that can make you feel tired, grumpy, or just kind of off. That's all normal. As you start to heal, you'll begin to feel more and more like you again. In the meantime, doing things you enjoy — like drawing, playing a game, or talking to someone you love — can help. And if this feeling really worries you, it's a great idea to talk to your parent or nurse about it.
What is the Heroes' Circle?

The Heroes' Circle is a super cool program where kids learn breathing exercises, relaxation techniques, and even some martial arts moves! They visit kids in the hospital every week, both in patient rooms and in the clinic. It's a fun way to feel strong and learn tricks that can help you feel calmer. You can ask your nurse about it or email info@kidskickingcancer.ca to learn more.
Can I bring my teddy bear to the hospital?

Absolutely! Bringing a favourite toy or stuffed animal from home can help you feel more comfortable. Just make sure it's clean before you bring it, and try not to share it with other kids in the hospital. Toys that can be wiped down or washed are the best kind to bring.
Do doctors and nurses live at the hospital?

Ha, it can seem like that sometimes! But no, doctors and nurses go home to their own families just like your family comes to visit you. They work in shifts — that means one group works during the day and another group takes over at night. That's why you might see different nurses at different times. But someone is always here to take care of you, 24 hours a day!
Someone gave us a special form to say nice things about a nurse. What was that?

That was probably information about the Great Moments Recognition Program! It's a way for patients and families to say thank you to staff members who made their hospital stay better. If someone on your care team was really kind or helpful, your family can fill out a short form on the LHSC website to recognize them. That person will get a special letter and a little gift to know that your family appreciated them. It's a really nice way to say thanks!
What are medical students?

Medical students are people who are still in school learning how to be doctors. They've already finished university and now they're doing extra years of special doctor school. They might help take care of you, but there's always a fully trained doctor watching over everything they do. It's kind of like having a student driver — there's always someone experienced right there with them!
I'm going to miss my friend's birthday party.

Oh, that's a real bummer. Missing something fun like a birthday party is hard, and it's okay to feel disappointed. But your friend will understand — they'd want you to get better more than anything. Maybe you could video call during the party, or your parent could help you make a card or pick out a little gift to give your friend later. And who knows — when you're better, maybe you two can have your own special celebration together!
What's that thing they clip on my arm that puffs up?

That's a blood pressure cuff! It wraps around your arm and puffs up with air to measure your blood pressure, which tells the nurse how well your heart is pumping blood around your body. It squeezes for a few seconds and then slowly lets go. It feels funny and tight, but it's totally harmless and over really quickly!
What is that garden outside?

That garden is called Alex's Butterfly Garden, and it's a beautiful, quiet outdoor space in Zone D on the second level. It has benches to sit on and a soothing water fountain. It was created for children, families, and staff to enjoy a peaceful spot for quiet memories and thinking. The garden is named in honour of babies who were very special. It's a lovely place to sit if you want some fresh air and a calm moment outside.
Someone offered to walk my dad to his car at night. Who was that?

That was a security guard! At Children's Hospital, the security team can walk family members to their car or even to the Ronald McDonald House if it's dark outside or someone doesn't feel safe walking alone. All your dad needs to do is call the security dispatch number, and they'll send someone to help. It's one of the ways the hospital looks after your whole family, not just you!
Can I sit on an empty hospital bed?

Even if a bed next to you looks empty, it needs to stay clean for the next child who might need it. So visitors and parents shouldn't sit on, put their feet on, or sleep in empty hospital beds. Your nurse can help find a comfortable chair for your visitors.
What happens during a bedside shift change?

A shift change is when one nurse finishes their work time and a new nurse starts. At Children's Hospital, the nurses do this right next to your bed! The new nurse will introduce themselves to you, and then the two nurses will talk about how you're doing and what the plan is for your care. They'll do some safety checks too. Your mom or dad can listen and even ask questions or share information. It takes about three to five minutes, and then your new nurse will let you know when they'll be back to check on you.
What does the doctor actually do compared to everyone else?

Your doctor — called the attending physician — is like the captain of the team. They look at the big picture of what's going on with your health, work with everyone else to make a plan, and make the final decisions about your care. They also supervise the residents and medical students. While nurses are with you the most and handle your day-to-day care, and other specialists help with specific things, your doctor is the one who puts all the puzzle pieces together.
Can I watch TV in my room?

Yes you can! The hospital has a patient entertainment site where you can watch live Rogers TV for free. If you have a streaming account like Netflix or Disney+, you can log in and watch your own shows too. There's free WiFi available, and your parent or caregiver can call 1-800-642-3958 if you need help connecting.
Why are there so many different people taking care of me?

Because you deserve the best team! At Children's Hospital, lots of different helpers work together to take care of every part of you — not just the part that's sick or hurt. Your doctor looks at the big picture, your nurse takes care of you day and night, a dietitian makes sure your food is right, a physiotherapist helps your body move, and a Child Life Specialist helps you feel happy and brave. Everyone has their own superpower, and together they make one amazing team!
What happens when the nurses change shifts?

When one nurse's shift is ending and a new nurse is starting, they do something called a bedside shift change. The new nurse will come to your room and introduce themselves. The two nurses will talk about how you're doing and what your care plan is. Your parent is invited to listen, ask questions, and share anything they think is important. It only takes about three to five minutes!
Who is the person at the front desk when we walked in?

That person is a volunteer or an information desk helper! At Children's Hospital, there are friendly volunteers near the entrances — like at the B1 entrance and the B2 lobby — who help people find their way around the hospital. They can tell you which floor to go to, help you read a map, or point you in the right direction. Think of them as the hospital's welcome team! They're there from 8 in the morning to 3 in the afternoon on weekdays.
Someone gave me a phone to call home. Who did that?

That was your nurse or another staff member! Children's Hospital has patient telephones that you can use for free to make local and toll-free calls. They want you to be able to stay in touch with your family and friends. You're also welcome to use your own cell phone if you have one. Staying connected to people you love is really important, especially when you're in the hospital!
Who are the people in the playroom?

The people helping out in the playroom could be Child Life Specialists or volunteers! Children's Hospital has some great play spaces, like the School-Age Activity Room on the sixth floor where you can do crafts, play board games, build with LEGO, and do puzzles. Child Life staff and volunteers plan fun activities and special events throughout the month. These helpers are there to make sure you have fun and feel more at home while you're in the hospital.
Where can I get a drink of water?

Ask your nurse! They can bring you water or let you know where to get it on your unit. On the B6 inpatient floor, there are pantries in B6-149 and B6-231 with drinks available. But always check with your care team first, because sometimes the doctors need you to wait before drinking.
I heard the doctors talking and they sounded serious. Am I dying?

Hearing doctors talk in serious voices can be really scary, especially when you don't understand everything they're saying. Doctors use their serious voice a lot because they're concentrating and being careful — it doesn't mean something terrible is happening. The most important thing is to talk to YOUR doctor or your parent about what you heard and what you're worried about. They will be honest with you and explain things in a way you can understand. Please don't keep this worry inside — the grown-ups on your team are there to answer your questions.
Who is the person who helped me practise talking?

That's a speech therapist! Speech therapists are part of your care team here at Children's Hospital. They help kids with things like talking, swallowing, and making sounds. They know lots of fun games and exercises to help your mouth and voice work their best. If you have questions about what you're practising together, your speech therapist is happy to explain!
What is the SMILE Room?

The SMILE Room is one of the coolest rooms in the hospital! It's on the sixth floor in room B6-261, and it's filled with amazing sensory stuff to help you relax or have fun. There are bubble columns that light up, fibre optic lights you can touch, mirrors, and music. It's designed to help kids feel calm and comfortable. If you'd like to visit the SMILE Room, ask your nurse or a Child Life Specialist — they can help you get there!
My mom keeps crying. Is it my fault she's sad?

Oh sweetie, it's absolutely not your fault that your mom is sad. Your mom cries because she loves you so, so much and she doesn't like seeing you in the hospital. Parents worry about their kids — that's just what parents do. But her tears aren't because of anything you did wrong. You being brave and working on getting better is actually the thing that helps her the most. If it makes you feel better, you could give her a hug or tell her you love her. You two are a team!
What is that thing on the wall that looks like a phone?

That's the patient telephone! You can use it to make calls to people in London or to toll-free numbers, and it's totally free. If you want to call your grandma or your best friend to tell them about your day, you can use it! Most kids also use their own cell phones, which is totally fine too. The hospital wants you to be able to stay in touch with the people you love while you're here.
Will someone help me if I don't understand what's happening?

Absolutely! You can always ask questions — any time, about anything. Your nurses, doctors, and especially the Child Life Specialists are there to explain things in a way that makes sense to you. If someone explains something and you still don't understand, it's totally okay to say 'Can you explain that differently?' Nobody will think that's silly. Your care team wants you to feel safe and know what's going on.
There's someone at the hospital who talks about feelings. Is that okay to do?

Absolutely! Talking about feelings is one of the bravest things you can do. At Children's Hospital, there are people whose whole job is helping kids with their feelings — like psychologists, social workers, and Child Life Specialists. Psychologists can help you learn tricks for dealing with worry, sadness, or frustration. Social workers help your whole family cope. And Child Life Specialists use play and activities to help you express yourself. You never have to keep big feelings bottled up. Talking about them is always okay.
Are there dogs in the hospital?

Sometimes, yes! Children's Hospital works with a group called St. John Ambulance to have therapy dogs visit patients. These dogs are specially trained to be gentle and calm, and petting them can make you feel really happy and relaxed. Ask your care team if there's a therapy dog visit coming up — they can let you know! Regular pet visits from home aren't usually allowed, but there can be special exceptions.
What happens before an operation?

Before an operation, your care team will explain everything to you and your family. You might have to stop eating and drinking for a little while before — your nurse will tell you when. You'll put on a hospital gown, and the team will check your armband to make sure everything is right. Children's Hospital even has a program where your mom or dad can sometimes come into the operating room with you while you fall asleep! It's called the PPI program. Your nurse or Child Life Specialist can tell you more about it.
What is that thing on my finger that glows red?

That little clip is called a pulse oximeter, and the red glow is just a tiny light! It shines through your finger to measure how much oxygen is in your blood. It doesn't hurt at all — it's just using light to peek at what's happening inside. Pretty cool, huh? If it feels uncomfortable, let your nurse know and they can adjust it.
What does the Social Worker do?

A social worker is someone at the hospital who helps your family with all the non-medical stuff that can be stressful. They can help your parents figure out paperwork, find support in your community, or just talk through how they're feeling. They're a really helpful person to know about, especially when your family needs extra support. Your nurse can connect your family with one!
Why do some rooms have two beds?

Some hospital rooms are shared between two patients. Each patient gets their own space with a curtain they can pull for privacy. The hospital tries to give you the room you'd like, but it depends on which rooms are available and sometimes on what kind of care you need. Even in a shared room, the nurses make sure you feel comfortable and looked after!
How many more sleeps until I go home?

That's one of the hardest questions in the hospital because sometimes even the doctors aren't sure exactly how many sleeps it'll be — it depends on how your body is doing. But you can ask your parent or nurse to check with the doctor on how things are going. Every day, your care team is watching how you're doing and thinking about the best time for you to go home. In the meantime, try to make each 'sleep' count by doing something fun or relaxing during the day. You're getting closer!
What is Upopolis?

Upopolis is a free, safe website just for kids aged 8 to 18 who are in hospitals across Canada. It lets you connect with other kids who are going through something similar. You can chat, share stories, and make friends. There are laptops you can borrow through Child Life Services to use it. Ask a Child Life Specialist if you want to check it out!
What is the button I can press to call the nurse?

There's a special button near your bed called the call button. When you press it, it sends a little signal to the nurses' station so they know you need help. It's kind of like ringing a doorbell! You can press it any time you need something — if you're thirsty, if something hurts, or if you just have a question. A nurse will come to your room to see how they can help. It's there for you, so don't be shy about using it!
Where is the hospital?

Children's Hospital is at 800 Commissioners Road East in London, Ontario. It's in Zone B of the Victoria Hospital site. If you're coming by car, the closest parking is Parking Lot 8, which is a big garage off Baseline Road.
Why does my nurse keep washing her hands so much?

Your nurse is a germ-fighting superhero! Washing hands is the BEST way to stop germs from spreading in the hospital. Your nurse cleans their hands before coming into your room, when they leave, and lots of times in between. They usually use a special hand gel called alcohol-based hand rub. Everyone who visits you — family, friends, and helpers — should wash their hands too. It keeps you and everyone else in the hospital safe and healthy!
Who is the person who makes sure my room is clean?

That's someone from the housekeeping team, also called environmental services. They come to your room to clean surfaces, take out trash, and make sure everything is tidy and germ-free. Keeping your room clean is one of the best ways to stop germs from spreading, and the hospital takes it very seriously. They might also ask your family to keep extra stuff to a minimum so they can clean every spot properly!
I saw a kid in a wheelchair. Will that happen to me?

It makes sense that seeing other kids with different equipment might make you wonder about your own situation. Every kid in the hospital is here for their own reason, and what's happening with one child is usually very different from what's happening with you. A wheelchair doesn't always mean something really serious — sometimes kids just use one to get around the hospital more easily. If you're worried about what might happen with your own health, the best thing to do is ask your doctor or your parent. They can answer your specific questions.
Who is the person who helped me when I was really sick and needed lots of machines?

That was the team in the Paediatric Critical Care Unit — the PCCU. When kids are very sick and need extra-close watching and lots of special equipment, they go to the PCCU where a team of specially trained doctors, nurses, and other helpers are there around the clock. There are even two sleep spaces right at your bedside so your family can stay close. The PCCU team is there for the sickest kids, and they work really hard to help you get better.
Is the person who takes my blood a doctor?

Not always! The person who takes your blood might be a nurse, a lab technician, or sometimes a doctor. Lab technicians are people who are specially trained to draw blood and run tests on it. After they take a little bit of your blood, they send it to a lab where scientists look at it to help your doctor understand what's happening in your body. Whoever takes your blood, they'll check your armband first to make sure everything is matched to you!
Can my brother or sister visit me?

Usually yes! Siblings can visit, but just like all visitors, they should wash their hands and shouldn't come if they're feeling sick. The hospital also asks visitors to check with the nurses first about the best times. Having your brother or sister visit can really cheer you up! The hospital also has some fun programs that siblings can be part of, like the Heroes' Circle.
Why does my bed go up and down?

Hospital beds are really special because they have a motor inside that lets them move! The nurses can raise or lower different parts of the bed using buttons. They might raise the head part so you can sit up to eat or watch TV, or raise the whole bed so it's easier for the nurse to take care of you. Sometimes your nurse might let you try the buttons yourself. It's like having a recliner that can do way more tricks!
Why does the doctor have a stethoscope?

A stethoscope is that cool instrument that hangs around a doctor's neck! When they put the round part on your chest or back, it lets them hear your heart beating and your lungs breathing. It works kind of like super-powered ears. It might feel a little cold when they first put it on you, but it doesn't hurt at all.
What is the Bravery Beads program?

Bravery Beads is a really special program at Children's Hospital! You get to collect beads that tell the story of everything you go through during your time at the hospital. Each bead represents something different — like a bead for getting a needle, a bead for an X-ray, or a bead for being brave during a procedure. You string them together to make your own personal necklace or collection. It's a way to remember how strong and brave you are! Any kid can join — just ask your nurse or a Child Life Specialist.
I don't like hospital food. I want my mom's food.

It's pretty normal to miss your favourite home-cooked meals — hospital food is different from what you're used to. But the kitchen here tries hard to make food that kids like, and they have lots of choices. Your parent can also bring food from home and store it in the family fridge on your unit. Just make sure to check with your nurse first, because sometimes the doctor needs you to eat a special diet to help you get better. If something about the food really bothers you, let your care team know and they'll try to help.
Nobody tells me what's happening. I want to know.

You have every right to know what's going on — it's your body! Sometimes grown-ups don't always think to explain everything to kids, but that doesn't mean you can't ask. You can tell your parent or your nurse that you want to understand what's happening and why. They can explain things in a way that makes sense. Knowing what's coming usually makes things feel a lot less scary. You're so smart for wanting to understand, and your care team should be happy to answer your questions.
What is the Sanctuary?

The Sanctuary is a very quiet, peaceful room where anyone can go for some calm time. It's in Zone C, on the third floor, in room C3-402. It's open all day and all night, so you can visit any time. People go there to think, pray, meditate, or just have some quiet time. It doesn't matter what religion you are or if you don't have a religion at all — everyone is welcome. If you or your family want a peaceful break, ask your nurse how to get there.
They said they have to do the test again because it didn't work. I don't want to!

Oh, I can really understand how frustrating that feels. You already got through it once, and hearing you have to do it again is really disappointing. It's okay to feel annoyed and upset. But the doctor needs the test to work properly so they can help you the best way possible. Your care team will do everything they can to make it go smoothly this time. Talk to your nurse about what happened and what they can do differently to make it easier. And remember — you've already proven you can do it. You're stronger than you know.
What if I'm scared to walk on the slippery floor?

That's totally understandable! The hospital wants to make sure you don't slip, so wear your non-slip socks, slippers, or shoes with good grip. If you need help walking around, press the nurse call button and someone will come to help you. You can also ask for a wheelchair if walking feels too tricky.
Why does the nurse scan my bracelet before giving me medicine?

Your bracelet has a barcode on it — just like the barcodes on items at the grocery store! When the nurse scans it, the computer checks to make sure the right medicine is going to the right patient. It's a super important safety step that happens every single time. Pretty smart system, right?
What is a thermometer?

A thermometer is a tool the nurse uses to check your temperature — that means finding out if your body is warmer than it should be. There are different kinds! Some go under your tongue, some go in your ear, and some just touch your forehead. It only takes a few seconds and doesn't hurt at all. If your body is too warm, it might mean you have a fever, and the doctors will want to know about it so they can help you feel better.
What does an IV look like?

An IV is a tiny, thin tube that goes into a vein in your hand or arm. It's connected to a bag of clear liquid that hangs on a tall pole with wheels. The liquid slowly drips down through the tube into your body. It's how the hospital gives you water, medicine, or other things your body might need. Getting the IV put in uses a small needle, but remember — the Comfort Promise means they'll use numbing cream and help you stay comfortable. Once it's in, the needle comes out and just a soft little tube stays.
Who's the person who prayed with my grandma?

That was most likely a Spiritual Care Specialist. Children's Hospital has people whose job is to support families with prayer, quiet time, and spiritual comfort — no matter what you or your family believe. There's even a special room called the Sanctuary on the third floor of Zone C where anyone can go for quiet time, prayer, or just to sit peacefully. If your grandma or your family wants to talk to a Spiritual Care Specialist again, your nurse can contact one for you.
What is the family lounge?

The family lounge is called the Culliton Family Lounge, and it's in room B6-110. It's a comfy space where you and your family or friends can hang out together and relax away from your hospital room. Sometimes the hospital holds special group events and family coffee hours there too. It's a nice place to take a little break!
What if my bracelet falls off?

If your armband comes off, tell your nurse right away! They'll put a new one on for you. That bracelet is really important because it has your name, birthday, and a barcode that they check before giving you any medicine or doing any tests. Don't worry — it happens sometimes, and getting a new one is quick.
This thing in my hand hurts. What is it?

That's called an IV, and it's a tiny little tube that helps get medicine or fluids into your body to help you feel better. It can feel a little sore or weird, especially when they first put it in. If it's hurting you right now, please tell your nurse right away — they need to know so they can check it and make sure everything is okay. Sometimes they can make it more comfortable or adjust it. You're being so brave for having it, and it's doing an important job helping your body heal.
What does a speech therapist do?

A speech therapist helps kids who have trouble talking, swallowing, or making certain sounds. At the hospital, they might work with you if your mouth or throat needs some extra help after a procedure, or if you're having trouble eating certain foods safely. They use games and exercises to make it fun. They're part of your care team and really good at what they do!
The doctor said I can go home soon but I'm nervous.

It's actually pretty normal to feel a little nervous about going home, even though you've been wanting to go! You've gotten used to having nurses and doctors nearby. But going home means you're doing well enough that you don't need all that extra help anymore — and that's a great thing! Your care team will give your parent all the instructions for taking care of you at home, and they'll tell you who to call if you have any questions. You're going to do great. And if you're worried about anything specific, ask your nurse before you leave.
Can I go outside during my stay?

That depends on your care plan. Some kids can visit outdoor spaces like Alex's Butterfly Garden. But always ask your nurse before going anywhere outside your room. They'll let you know if it's safe for you to take a little trip outside.
Can my little brother visit?

Your little brother can come visit! The hospital just asks that visitors check with the nurses about the best time to come, and that he doesn't visit if he's been feeling sick in the past week. An adult should be with him the whole time, and everyone should wash their hands when they come in and when they leave.
Why does the nurse wear gloves sometimes?

Nurses wear gloves to protect both you and themselves from germs. The gloves are clean and new every time — they put on a fresh pair before doing things like checking your IV or helping with a bandage, and then they throw them away after. Sometimes the nurse might also wear a special gown or a mask. This is all part of keeping germs from spreading. It might look a little different, but it's a good thing!
I'm so bored. There's nothing to do here.

Being stuck in a hospital room can definitely get boring. But there are actually more things to do than you might think! Children's Hospital has activity rooms with crafts, board games, puzzles, and LEGO. There are Child Life Specialists who plan fun activities and special events. There's even a nature-themed playroom called Ashley's Backyard and a cool SMILE Room with bubble columns and fibre optic lights! Ask your nurse what's available and when you can go explore. And you can always bring your own books, games, or watch something on the entertainment site.
Who is the person with the name tag who asked my name and birthday?

That could be any member of your care team — a nurse, a doctor, a therapist, or someone else helping to take care of you. They ask your name and birthday a lot, and that might seem kind of funny, but it's one of the most important ways they keep you safe! They check your armband and ask you these questions before giving medicine, doing tests, or taking you anywhere. It's like a secret password that makes sure everything is just right for YOU.
Can I do art while I'm here?

Yes! Children's Hospital has an Art Therapy program. An art therapist can help you draw, paint, or create things as a way to express how you're feeling. You don't have to be a great artist — it's all about having fun and getting your feelings out. It can be really relaxing too. Ask your nurse or a Child Life Specialist about it!
What will I eat at the hospital?

The hospital has food for you! Breakfast comes around 7:45 in the morning, lunch is around 11:45, and dinner comes around 4:45 in the afternoon. A menu will come on your breakfast tray so you can pick what you'd like to eat the next day — kind of like ordering from a restaurant! If you have any allergies or special foods you need, just tell your nurse and they'll make sure your meals are right for you. Your grown-up can also get food from the Tim Hortons in the hospital.
What is that thing that squeezes my finger?

That clip on your finger is called a pulse oximeter. It uses a little red light to see how much oxygen your blood is carrying. Oxygen is what you breathe in, and your blood carries it all around your body. The clip just checks that everything is moving along the way it should. It doesn't hurt — it just clips on gently and does its thing!
There's a person who came with a translator for my family. Who set that up?

Someone on your care team arranged that! Children's Hospital offers free interpretation services, which means they can get someone to translate for your family so everyone can understand what the doctors and nurses are saying. It's really important that your family can communicate in a language they're comfortable with. If your family ever needs a translator again, just ask your nurse or anyone on your care team — they'll set it up.
What's a dietitian?

A dietitian is a food expert! At the hospital, the dietitian makes sure you're getting the right kinds of foods to help your body heal and feel strong. If you have allergies or need a special diet, they're the person who helps figure out what's safe and yummy for you to eat. If you have any questions about your food, your nurse can ask the dietitian to come chat with you.
When can I go home? I want to go now.

Wanting to go home is one of the most normal feelings in the world, especially when you've been in the hospital for a while. Your doctor is the person who decides when it's safe for you to leave, and they're working hard to get you there. It might not happen as fast as you'd like, but every day your body is getting a little better. You can ask your parent or nurse what the plan is — they can help you understand what needs to happen before you can go. Hang in there — you're doing great!
What is that machine that goes 'whoosh' sound?

There are a few machines that make whooshing sounds! One common one is the blood pressure machine — it makes a whooshing sound when it pumps air into the cuff on your arm. Another might be a suction machine that helps clear fluids. If you hear a sound that you're curious or worried about, just ask your nurse! They'll tell you exactly what it is and why it's there.
Someone asked me if I wanted to join a research study. What does that mean?

That person was probably a doctor or a researcher. A research study is when the hospital is trying to learn new things about how to help kids get better. They might ask your family if you'd like to be part of it, but you absolutely do NOT have to say yes. It's completely your choice, and if you say no, your care won't change at all. Your parents can read all about the study and take their time deciding. Nobody will be upset if the answer is no.
Who is the person who helped my mom figure out how to give me medicine at home?

That was probably a pharmacist or your nurse. At Children's Hospital, the pharmacy is on the first floor near the B1 entrance and is open on weekdays. Before you go home, a pharmacist can make a medicine calendar for your family that shows exactly when to give each medicine and how much. Your nurse also goes over all the medicine instructions. If anything is confusing, your family can always ask the pharmacist to explain it again — that's what they're there for!
What is the Paediatric Family Resource Centre?

The Paediatric Family Resource Centre is a special room on the 1st floor of Zone B, room B1-006. It's a quiet place where your parents can find information about your health, get help filling out forms, and talk to people who have been through similar experiences. It's open most days of the week. Your family can pop in anytime during its open hours!
What happens if I feel dizzy after a procedure?

Feeling a little dizzy or woozy after a procedure is normal for some kids. Your nurse knows this might happen and will keep a close eye on you. They'll make sure you stay in bed until you feel steady, and the bed rails will be up to keep you safe. If you feel dizzy, tell your nurse right away — you don't have to be brave about it! They can help you feel better. Drinking water and resting usually helps the dizziness go away.
Who is Ollie the Clown?

Ollie is a really special person at Children's Hospital! Ollie is a therapeutic clown, which means Ollie is specially trained to make kids laugh, play games, and have fun while they're in the hospital. Ollie helps make hospital days feel a little more normal and a lot more silly. If you see Ollie around, get ready to smile!
I heard an alarm going off and it scared me.

Alarms in the hospital can sound really startling! But most of the time, alarms are just machines letting the nurses know that something small needs attention — like an IV bag that needs to be changed, or a sensor that moved out of place. It's kind of like a doorbell ringing. The nurses know exactly what to do when they hear those alarms. If an alarm near you goes off and it scares you, you can ask your nurse to explain what it was. Most of the time, it's nothing to worry about.
Someone from the hospital talked to my family about keeping our culture's traditions. Who was that?

That might have been a Spiritual Care Specialist, a social worker, or the Youth Indigenous Wellness Consultant if your family is Indigenous. Children's Hospital cares about your family's cultural customs and religious beliefs, and they want to make sure those are respected during your stay. There's also an Indigenous Healing Space in the hospital for First Nations, Inuit, Métis, and Urban Indigenous families. Your care team is always happy to talk about ways to honour your family's traditions.
What is the Sanctuary?

The Sanctuary is a very quiet, peaceful room in Zone C, level 3, room C3-402. It's open all day and all night for anyone who wants some quiet time, whether for praying, thinking, or just being calm. All patients and families are welcome there, no matter what they believe. It's a really nice place to go when you want a moment of peace.
There's someone who helps families who need extra help because of how the world treats them. Who is that?

That might be a Black Health Navigator. Children's Hospital has trained health-care workers called Black Health Navigators who help Black patients and families navigate the hospital. They make sure your family's voice is heard and that you get the care you need. They can explain your health-care options and go with you to meetings with your care team. If you'd like to connect with a Black Health Navigator, ask your care team or check out the hospital's website.
What happens if my family speaks another language?

Children's Hospital has interpreters who can help! If your family is more comfortable speaking a language other than English, you can ask your care team for an interpreter — and it's totally free. The hospital knows it's really important for your family to understand everything the doctors and nurses are saying, and for the doctors to understand your family too. Just let your nurse know what language you need, and they'll arrange for help.
The parking garage was dark and scary when we came in.

Parking garages can feel a bit gloomy, especially when you're already nervous about going to the hospital. But the one at Children's Hospital — Parking Lot 8 — has people around and security guards who can help if you ever feel unsafe. Next time, if the parking garage feels too much, you can ask your parent to drop you off at the main entrance first and then go park. And once you're inside the hospital, it's bright and there are friendly people ready to help. You did great getting here!
There was someone in my room wearing gloves and a gown. Are they sick?

No, they're not sick at all! Sometimes people at the hospital wear extra things like gloves, a gown, or a mask to keep germs from spreading around. It's kind of like wearing a raincoat to keep dry in the rain — except this keeps germs away. It's actually a really smart way to keep you AND them healthy. Your nurse or doctor can explain why someone might need to wear that extra gear when they visit you.
What is an MRI?

An MRI is a machine that takes really detailed pictures of the inside of your body. It's a big tube-shaped machine, and you lie on a flat bed that slides inside it. The machine makes loud knocking and buzzing sounds — kind of like a drum beat! They'll give you special headphones or ear plugs so the noise isn't too loud. The most important thing is to lie really still, like a statue. It doesn't hurt at all, but it might feel a little strange being in a small space. Your family will be nearby the whole time.
I miss my house. I want to go home.

I bet you do — your home is your favourite place, and it makes sense that you'd miss it. Being in the hospital can feel really different from what you're used to. But guess what? You can bring little pieces of home with you. Your family can bring your favourite stuffed animal, a blanket, or some pictures to put near your bed. And your family can visit you and stay with you too. The doctors and nurses are working hard to help you feel better so you can get home as soon as possible.
Who's the person who took my picture with a big machine?

That was a medical imaging technician or technologist! They use special machines to take pictures of the inside of your body — like your bones, your tummy, or your head. It's kind of like a camera, but instead of taking a picture of your face, it takes a picture of what's going on inside you. These pictures help your doctor figure out the best way to help you. The technician is specially trained to use the machine and make sure you're comfortable.
Someone gave my mom directions to a special room with toys. Who was that?

That might have been a Child Life Specialist, a volunteer, or your nurse! Children's Hospital has some really fun spaces. There's Ashley's Backyard on the sixth floor, which is a nature-themed playroom for younger kids. There's also a School-Age Activity Room with crafts, board games, puzzles, and LEGO. And there's even a SMILE Room with bubble columns, fibre optics, mirrors, and music! Your care team can help you find the play spaces that are open for you.
Why can't people visit if they're sick?

When someone has a cold or a tummy bug, they carry germs that could spread to kids in the hospital. Since many kids here are already not feeling well, catching extra germs could make them feel a whole lot worse. That's why the hospital asks people who are feeling sick to wait until they're better before visiting. It's a way of being a really good friend — protecting others by staying home until you're well!
What is the bracelet they put on my arm?

That bracelet is called an armband, and it's really important! It has your name, your birthday, a special hospital number, and a little barcode on it — kind of like the barcodes on things at the grocery store. Before anyone gives you medicine or does a test, they'll look at your bracelet to make sure they have the right person. It doesn't hurt to wear it, and it helps keep you safe the whole time you're at the hospital.
How does my room number work?

Hospital room numbers are like a little code! If your room is B2-503, here's what it means: the 'B' is the zone (like a section of the hospital), the '2' is the floor number, and '503' is your room. So B2-503 means room 503 on the second floor of Zone B. Pretty cool, right?
Why are there so many different people taking care of me?

Each person on your care team is an expert at something different. Your doctor figures out what's going on with your body. Your nurse takes care of you every day and checks how you're feeling. There might also be a physiotherapist who helps you move, a dietitian who makes sure you're eating the right foods, and more. They all work together like a team to take the best care of you!
Can I play with the toys in the playroom?

Yes! The activity rooms are there for you to enjoy. The School-Age Activity Room has board games, puzzles, LEGO, and crafts. Child Life staff and volunteers also plan fun activities and special events there during the month. Just make sure a grown-up knows where you are when you go.
Who is the person who put the tiny bracelet on my baby brother?

That was a nurse in the NICU or the unit where your baby brother is staying. Babies under one year old get a regular armband AND a small security alarm band. The alarm band helps keep tiny babies extra safe — it's like a little protector that makes sure your baby brother stays exactly where he's supposed to be. It's one of the special ways the hospital watches over the very littlest patients!
What is art therapy?

Art therapy is a really cool program at Children's Hospital where you get to express your feelings through art! You might draw, paint, or make things with craft supplies. A special art therapist works with you, and you don't have to be good at art — it's not about making something perfect. It's about having fun, relaxing, and letting your feelings out in a creative way. Art therapy can help you feel more in control and less stressed while you're in the hospital. Ask your care team if you'd like to try it!
What is an ultrasound?

An ultrasound is a way for doctors to look inside your body using sound waves — not the kind of sound you can hear, though! The person doing the ultrasound will put some warm, squishy gel on your skin and then gently move a smooth wand over it. On a screen nearby, a picture will appear showing what's inside your body. It doesn't hurt at all! The gel might feel a little cold and gooey, but you can wipe it off when it's done. It's kind of like seeing a secret picture of what's going on inside you.
Where is the pharmacy?

The pharmacy at Children's Hospital is on the first floor in room B1-001, right next to the B1 entrance. It's open Monday to Friday from 8 in the morning until 5:30 in the evening. If the doctor gives you a prescription before you go home, your family can get it filled right there so you don't have to make another stop! The pharmacist there can also answer questions about your medicines.
What does the B in my room number mean?

The letter in your room number tells you which zone of the hospital you're in! Children's Hospital is in Zone B. So if your room number starts with B, that means you're right here in the children's part. The number after the letter tells you which floor you're on. For example, B2-503 means Zone B, floor 2, room 503. It's like an address inside the hospital!
Is there an outdoor space to play?

There's Alex's Butterfly Garden on Level 2 of Zone D — it has benches and a nice water fountain. It's not exactly a playground, but it's a beautiful, calming outdoor spot where you can enjoy being outside for a little while. Ask your nurse if you're allowed to go!
I'm going to miss my friends at school.

Missing your friends is totally normal — they're probably missing you too! The good news is you can still keep in touch. You can use the phone by your bed to call them, and if you have a tablet or phone, you can video chat. Children's Hospital even has free Wi-Fi so you can stay connected. And when you're feeling up to it, there are activity rooms where you might meet other kids who are here too. Your friends will be so happy to see you when you're feeling better and ready to go back to school.
Can I bring my teddy bear to the hospital?

Yes, you can bring your teddy bear! Children's Hospital says you can bring a few favourite toys, books, and even family pictures to help you feel more at home. Just make sure your teddy is clean before you bring it — wipeable or washable toys are the best. The hospital asks that you don't bring too many things, and that you don't share your toys with other kids in the hospital, because that helps stop germs from spreading. But your teddy is welcome to stay right with you!
Can I use the bathroom in another kid's room?

No, visitors should use a different bathroom, not the one in a patient's room. This is to help stop germs from spreading between patients. Your nurse can tell you where the closest bathroom for visitors is.
Can I pick what I want to eat?

Yes, kind of! At breakfast, you'll get a form where you can pick what you'd like to eat for the next day. The choices will depend on what your doctor says is okay for you. The hospital can make lots of different kinds of food, including vegetarian and food for allergies. If you have a favourite food or something you really don't like, let your nurse know!
What is a Child Life Specialist?

A Child Life Specialist is someone whose whole job is to help kids feel less scared and more comfortable in the hospital. They can explain what's going to happen before a procedure, teach you ways to feel brave, and play games with you. They're kind of like a hospital buddy who's an expert at making things less worrying. You can ask your nurse to set up a visit with one!
Why can't I get out of bed? I want to play!

I know it's really frustrating to be stuck in bed when you just want to run around and play. Your body needs some rest right now to help it get better, and your doctor wants to make sure you're safe. But that doesn't mean you can't have any fun! There are things you can do right in your bed — like drawing, playing games on a tablet, reading, or doing puzzles. You can ask your nurse when it might be okay to get up, and a Child Life Specialist might be able to bring some fun activities to you.
I miss my dog. Can he come visit me?

Aw, I bet you miss your furry friend a lot! Dogs are the best cuddle buddies. At Children's Hospital, family pets usually can't come visit because they want to keep all the kids here healthy and safe. But sometimes, in really special situations, the hospital might be able to work something out — your parent can ask your care team about it. In the meantime, maybe your family can bring you a picture of your dog to put by your bed, or you could video call someone at home so you can see your pup on screen!
I don't understand why I have to stay here.

That's a really fair question, and it's okay to feel confused. Sometimes our bodies need extra help to feel better, and the hospital is the best place for that because it has all the special tools and people who know how to help. Your doctor and your parents can explain more about why you need to stay — it's always okay to ask them. Nothing is being hidden from you. The goal is to get you feeling good again and back home as soon as it's safe.
Can I watch TV?

Yes! The hospital has a patient entertainment site where you can watch live Rogers TV for free. If your family has a streaming account — like Netflix or Disney+ — you can log in to that too. Ask your nurse or a staff member if you need help getting it set up.
Why do they keep asking me my name and birthday?

Great question! The nurses and doctors ask your name and birthday a lot because they want to make really, really sure they're helping the right kid. It's one of the ways the hospital keeps you safe. Even though they already know who you are, checking is like double-checking your homework — it just makes sure everything is exactly right. So don't worry if they ask you again and again. It means they're being extra careful with you!
I have to get an X-ray. Will it hurt?

Here's the good news — X-rays don't hurt at all! You won't feel a single thing. The machine just takes a picture of the inside of your body, kind of like a camera but instead of taking a picture of your face, it takes a picture of your bones. You just have to lie still or stand still for a few seconds while it takes the picture. It's super quick. The room might look big and have some interesting equipment, but none of it touches you in a way that hurts. You've got this!
Where are the vending machines?

The vending machines are near the elevators in Zone B on the 1st and 3rd floors. There are ATMs there too if your parent needs cash. For a bigger meal, there's Tim Hortons on the second floor of Zone B.
Who decides when I can go home?

Your doctor — called the attending physician — is the main person who decides when you're well enough to go home. But they don't decide alone! They talk to your nurses, and sometimes other people on your care team like a physiotherapist or social worker, to make sure you're truly ready. Your family is part of that conversation too. Your care team will give your family all the instructions you need before you leave so everything goes smoothly at home.
What's a psychologist? Someone said they were one.

A psychologist is a person who is trained to help with feelings and thinking. At Children's Hospital, psychologists help kids and families deal with the tough parts of being sick or in the hospital. They can teach you tricks for handling worry, sadness, or frustration. They might also check how well you're learning and thinking if your medical condition affects those things. If you're ever feeling overwhelmed, a psychologist is a great person to talk to — and your nurse can help set up a visit.
Where can I get snacks?

If you get hungry between meals, there are a few places to find snacks! The ward you're staying on might have a family pantry with drinks and light snacks — on the sixth floor, the pantries are in rooms B6-149 and B6-231. There are also vending machines near the elevators on the first and third floors of Zone B. And your grown-up can go to the Tim Hortons on the second floor of Zone B, which is open on weekdays from 6:30 in the morning until 8 at night. Always check with your nurse before eating, just to make sure it's okay!
I don't want anyone to visit me. I look sick.

That's a completely okay feeling to have. You get to decide who visits you and when. If you're not feeling up to visitors right now, your parent can let people know that you need some quiet time. Nobody will be upset about that — the people who care about you want what's best for you. And when you are ready for visitors, they'll be happy to see you no matter how you look. Right now, your only job is to rest and get better at your own pace.
Will my brothers or sisters be able to visit me?

Your brothers and sisters can come visit you! Children's Hospital wants you to have the support of your family and friends. Visitors should check with the unit staff about the best times to visit. Everyone who visits should wash their hands or use hand sanitizer when they arrive. The hospital asks that nobody visits if they're feeling sick. During nighttime hours between 8 p.m. and 8 a.m., visitors should stay in your room and let the staff know they're there.
What if my test says something bad?

Waiting for test results can feel really nerve-wracking — the not knowing is often the hardest part. It's okay to feel anxious about it. Whatever the results say, your doctors will know what to do, and they'll explain everything to you and your family. You won't have to deal with it alone. Try not to imagine the worst thing before you even know what happened — sometimes our brains jump to scary places that aren't real. For now, try to do something that takes your mind off it, and let the grown-ups on your care team do the worrying.
What is a volunteer?

Volunteers are really kind people who come to the hospital to help out, even though it's not their job. Some volunteers help families find their way around the hospital, and some help out in playrooms or bring fun activities to kids. At Children's Hospital, you can find guide volunteers near the B1 entrance and B2 lobby. They wear special badges so you can spot them!
What is the call button for?

The call button is like a magic button that lets your nurse know you need something! It's usually near your bed. When you press it, a light goes on at the nurses' station and they come to check on you. You can press it anytime — if you're thirsty, if something hurts, if you need to go to the bathroom, or even if you just have a question. That's what it's there for!
Why do the doors lock at night?

Some doors in the hospital lock at certain times to help keep everyone safe, especially at night when it's quieter. The main entrance to the B Tower is open from 6:00 in the morning until 8:30 at night. After that, security guards are at the doors to make sure only the right people come in. It's like how you lock your front door at home — it helps everyone inside feel safe and protected.
What is the Information Desk?

The Information Desk is a spot where friendly staff and volunteers can help you and your family find your way around the hospital, answer questions, and point you in the right direction. The desks are open from 8 in the morning to 8 at night on weekdays, and from noon to 4 in the afternoon on weekends. There are also guide volunteers near the B1 entrance and B2 lobby on weekdays until 3 p.m. If you're ever not sure where to go, these are great people to ask!
My tummy hurts really bad. Make it stop.

Oh no, I'm really sorry your tummy is hurting. That sounds really uncomfortable. The most important thing you can do right now is tell your nurse or your mom or dad exactly how it feels — is it a sharp hurt or a squeezy hurt? Does it come and go? Your doctor and nurse are the ones who can help figure out what's going on and make it better. You're being so brave, and it's always the right thing to speak up about pain. Let's make sure a grown-up on your care team knows right away, okay?
What's an MRI? I heard I need one and it sounds scary.

An MRI is a machine that takes really detailed pictures of the inside of your body — like a super-powered camera. It doesn't hurt at all! You lie on a special table that slides into a big tube, and the machine makes some loud buzzing and knocking noises while it works. You'll get headphones or ear plugs to help with the noise, and some kids even get to listen to music. The hardest part is holding still, which is like being a statue. Your care team can tell you more about what your MRI will be like, so make sure to ask questions!
Can I watch TV in the hospital?

Yes, you can! Children's Hospital has a special entertainment site where you can watch Rogers TV for free. If your family has a streaming service like Netflix or Disney+, you can log in with your own account and watch your favourite shows too! There are also patient telephones you can use to call people for free if they're local or toll-free numbers. And you're welcome to use your own phone or tablet to stay connected with friends and family.
